When the Lorenz curve coincides with the 45-degree line, A = 0 and Gini = 0; when one individual holds all income, B = 0 and Gini = 1.

ref: NCERT Class XI Indian Economic Development; Todaro & Smith, Economic Development (Ch. 5: Poverty, Inequality, and Development)

stem: With reference to the axiomatic properties and structural limitations of the Gini coefficient as a measure of economic inequality, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Gini coefficient satisfies scale invariance and population independence, meaning it remains unchanged if every individual's income is multiplied by an identical positive constant or if the population is replicated proportionately.

2. In accordance with the Pigou-Dalton transfer principle, any rank-preserving progressive transfer of income from a richer individual to a poorer individual necessarily decreases the Gini coefficient.

3. Because the Gini coefficient uniquely characterizes the underlying income distribution, any two economies that record the exact same Gini coefficient must possess identical Lorenz curves and decile-wise income shares.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Gini coefficient satisfies core inequality axioms (anonymity, scale invariance, population independence, and the Pigou-Dalton transfer principle), it is an aggregate area metric that cannot distinguish between different distributional shapes when Lorenz curves intersect.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Scale invariance (mean independence) ensures that if all incomes double—or are converted from rupees to dollars—relative income shares and the Gini coefficient remain unchanged, even though absolute income gaps widen. Population independence (replication invariance) ensures that cloning the exact same economy N times does not alter its Gini coefficient.

Statement 2 is correct. The Pigou-Dalton transfer principle states that a transfer of income from a richer person to a poorer person (that does not reverse their relative ranks) strictly shifts the Lorenz curve inward toward the 45-degree line of equality, reducing the Gini coefficient. Notably, because the Gini depends on rank weights, it is most sensitive to transfers occurring near the mode (middle) of the income distribution.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The Gini coefficient only measures the aggregate geometric area between the Lorenz curve and the diagonal; it does not uniquely map to a single Lorenz curve. Two economies can have the exact same Gini coefficient with intersecting Lorenz curves—for example, Economy X may have a destitute bottom decile but an egalitarian middle-to-top distribution, while Economy Y has a well-protected bottom half but extreme concentration within the top 1%.

ref: Debraj Ray, Development Economics (Ch. 6: Economic Inequality); Amartya Sen, On Economic Inequality

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the measurement of economic inequality in India:
items: Statement-I: In India, the Gini coefficient derived from Household Consumption Expenditure Surveys (HCES) is systematically lower than the Gini coefficient for household income, which in turn is markedly lower than the Gini coefficient for household wealth.

Statement-II: Higher-income deciles exhibit a significantly higher Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) and a lower propensity to save than the bottom deciles, which compresses the dispersion of consumption across households.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Inequality monotonically increases as measurement moves from consumption to income to wealth because poorer households consume nearly all (or more than) their current income for subsistence, whereas richer households save a rising share of income that compounds into concentrated wealth stocks.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Across empirical studies in India (including NSSO HCES data, IHDS income panels, and AIDIS wealth surveys), consumption Gini (~0.25–0.30) is consistently lower than income Gini (~0.50–0.60), which in turn is lower than wealth Gini (~0.65–0.75+). Households smooth consumption over time, and basic biological subsistence establishes a floor on consumption at the bottom.

Statement-II is incorrect. By Keynes's psychological law of consumption, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) declines as income rises. Poorer deciles have a very high MPC (often near or exceeding 1 through borrowing/dissaving or public transfers to meet basic nutritional needs), whereas the richest deciles have a much lower MPC and a high Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS). Because the rich save a large share of their income rather than consuming it, consumption is far less unequal than income, and those accumulated savings compound across generations to make wealth inequality higher still.

ref: MoSPI Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) Fact Sheets; Economic Survey of India; NSSO All-India Debt and Investment Survey (AIDIS)

stem: In the context of advanced statistical metrics used to evaluate income inequality beyond the Gini coefficient, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Palma Ratio : Ratio of the total income received by the richest 20% of the population to that received by the poorest 20%
2. Quintile Ratio (S80/S20) : Ratio of the national income share of the richest 10% of the population to that of the poorest 40%, based on the empirical stability of the middle five deciles
3. Theil Index : Information-entropy-based inequality measure that can be additively decomposed into mutually exclusive within-group and between-group inequality components
4. Atkinson Index : Normative welfare-based inequality metric that incorporates an explicit weighting parameter representing society's degree of aversion to inequality
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Because the Gini coefficient is overly sensitive to the middle of the distribution and is not cleanly decomposable across subgroups, economists supplement it with tail-focused ratios (Palma), entropy-decomposable indices (Theil), and explicitly normative welfare indices (Atkinson).

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched (swapped with Quintile Ratio). Developed by Jose Gabriel Palma, the Palma Ratio is the ratio of the national income share of the top 10% to that of the bottom 40%. It rests on Palma's empirical observation that the middle 50% (deciles 5 to 9) almost universally capture roughly half of gross national income across countries, so distributional politics is essentially a contest between the richest 10% and poorest 40%.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched (swapped with Palma Ratio). The Quintile Ratio (S80/S20) simply divides the average or total income of the richest quintile (top 20%) by that of the poorest quintile (bottom 20%).

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Derived from Claude Shannon's information theory by Henri Theil, the Theil Index (a member of the Generalized Entropy class) possesses the crucial property of strict additive decomposability—unlike the Gini coefficient, total national inequality in the Theil index can be exactingly partitioned into 'between-group' inequality (e.g., rural vs. urban, or across states) and 'within-group' inequality.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Developed by Anthony Barnes Atkinson, the Atkinson Index incorporates an explicit normative inequality-aversion parameter (epsilon >= 0). As epsilon rises, the index places progressively greater weight on income transfers at the bottom end of the distribution, measuring the fraction of total national income that society would be willing to sacrifice to achieve an equally distributed equivalent income.

ref: UNDP Human Development Report (Technical Notes on Inequality-adjusted HDI); Debraj Ray, Development Economics

stem: With reference to the Kuznets Curve and the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC), consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Simon Kuznets' structural transformation hypothesis, income inequality initially rises during early industrialization as labor shifts from a low-productivity agricultural sector to a higher-productivity industrial sector.
2. Both the traditional Kuznets Curve and the Environmental Kuznets Curve postulate an inverted U-shaped relationship with per capita income plotted on the horizontal axis.

3. The downward-sloping phase of the Environmental Kuznets Curve proves that high GDP growth automatically reverses all forms of environmental degradation without requiring regulatory intervention or technological shifts.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Kuznets Curve attributes early-stage inequality growth to inter-sectoral labor migration during industrialization, while the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) applies a similar inverted U-shape to pollution. Crucially, the downward phase of the EKC is not an automatic consequence of GDP growth alone; it relies on induced policy regulations, cleaner technologies, and structural shifts toward services.

exp.why: Simon Kuznets (1955) explained that in dual-economy development, rural agricultural economies have low average incomes and low internal inequality, whereas urban industrial sectors have higher productivity and wider wage dispersion. As workers initially migrate to industry, between-sector inequality widens aggregate inequality until a majority of the workforce has transitioned and rural-urban wage gaps narrow.

Both curves depict an inverted U-shaped trajectory with per capita income on the horizontal (X) axis and income inequality (Gini coefficient) or environmental degradation/pollution per capita on the vertical (Y) axis.

In environmental economics (Grossman and Krueger framework), economic growth initially degrades the environment via the 'scale effect' (higher resource extraction and emissions). The subsequent downturn requires the 'composition effect' (shift to cleaner service industries) and 'technique effect' (R&D and cleaner technology), which are driven by stringent environmental regulations, institutional quality, and citizen demand rather than automatic GDP expansion. Moreover, global stock pollutants like CO2 and biodiversity loss do not automatically decline with income.

ref: Todaro & Smith, Economic Development, Ch. 5; Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh, Growth and Development

stem: In an economy experiencing a persistent divergence where the average real rate of return on capital (r) exceeds the real rate of economic growth (g), accompanied by a secular decline in the share of wages in Gross Value Added (GVA), which of the following macroeconomic outcomes is most likely to occur in the absence of redistributive policies?

opts.A: Accumulated wealth grows faster than national output, while the economy's aggregate marginal propensity to consume tends to decline due to the shift in functional income distribution toward capital owners.
opts.B: A declining share of labor income in GVA raises the economy-wide marginal propensity to consume, as capital owners spend a larger fraction of their incremental income on consumer goods than wage earners.
opts.C: The capital-to-income ratio converges toward zero in the long run, as high returns on capital induce firms to substitute labor for capital across all production sectors.
opts.D: The Gini coefficient of wealth distribution falls below the Gini coefficient of wage income, since higher capital returns broaden retail equity participation across lower-income deciles.

core: Under Thomas Piketty's r > g hypothesis, when the rate of return on capital exceeds the economic growth rate, past accumulated wealth recapitalizes faster than output and wages grow, intensifying wealth concentration. Simultaneously, a falling wage share in GVA shifts functional income toward profit/capital owners who have a lower marginal propensity to consume (MPC) than wage earners, depressing aggregate consumption demand.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct: When r > g, holders of existing capital need only reinvest a fraction of their capital income for their wealth stock to grow faster than the overall economy (g) and labor wages, widening wealth inequality. Furthermore, because wage earners have a significantly higher marginal propensity to consume (MPC) than owners of capital (who have a higher marginal propensity to save), a declining wage share in GVA dampens economy-wide aggregate consumption propensity. Option (B) is incorrect (T2 directional trap) because capital owners have a lower, not higher, MPC than wage earners. Option (C) is incorrect because under Piketty's Second Fundamental Law of Capitalism (beta = s/g), a low growth rate g relative to savings s increases, rather than eliminates, the long-run capital-to-income ratio. Option (D) is incorrect because wealth distribution is structurally much more unequal (higher Gini) than wage income distribution, and r > g further widens this gap.

ref: Thomas Piketty, Capital in the Twenty-First Century; Economic Survey of India (Inequality and Growth Chapters)

stem: With reference to poverty measurement metrics and consumption expenditure survey methodologies, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Poverty Gap Index measures the depth of poverty by averaging the proportionate income shortfall from the poverty line, the Squared Poverty Gap Index captures the severity of poverty by assigning greater weight to larger shortfalls.

2. A regressive income transfer from the poorest individual to an individual situated just below the poverty line that lifts the latter above the poverty line reduces both the Headcount Ratio and the Squared Poverty Gap Index.

3. Under the Modified Mixed Reference Period (MMRP) used in household consumption expenditure surveys, expenditure on frequently purchased perishable food items is recorded over a 365-day recall period, whereas expenditure on clothing and durables is recorded over a 7-day recall period.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In the Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) class of poverty measures, the Headcount Ratio (P0) captures incidence, the Poverty Gap Index (P1) captures depth, and the Squared Poverty Gap Index (P2) captures severity by squaring proportionate shortfalls to reflect inequality among the poor. In survey design, MMRP uses a 7-day recall for perishable food, 365-day recall for low-frequency durables/clothing, and 30-day recall for other items.

exp.why: The Poverty Gap Index (FGT P1) measures the average proportionate distance of poor households below the poverty line (depth of poverty), but it is insensitive to income redistribution among the poor. The Squared Poverty Gap Index (FGT P2) squares each poor person's proportionate shortfall, thereby placing a higher weight on the poorest of the poor and capturing poverty severity.

While taking money from the poorest person and giving it to someone just below the poverty line to push them above the threshold perversely reduces the Headcount Ratio (P0, which violates the transfer axiom), it increases the Squared Poverty Gap Index (P2). Because P2 weights the shortfall of the poorest person much more heavily than the tiny shortfall of the person just below the line, worsening the poorest person's deprivation increases P2.

Statement 3 reverses the recall periods of the Modified Mixed Reference Period (MMRP). Under MMRP (adopted by the Rangarajan Committee and NSSO Household Consumption Expenditure Surveys), high-frequency perishable food items (edible oil, vegetables, fruits, fish, meat, spices) use a short 7-day recall period to minimize recall lapse, low-frequency items (clothing, footwear, durables, education, institutional medical care) use a 365-day recall period, and all remaining items use a 30-day recall period.

ref: NITI Aayog / Rangarajan Committee Report on Poverty Measurement; Todaro & Smith Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and NITI Aayog's National Multidimensional Poverty Index (NMPI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the Global MPI which evaluates poverty across three dimensions, NITI Aayog's NMPI introduces a fourth equally weighted dimension on Digital and Financial Inclusion, assigning each dimension a weight of 25%.

2. NITI Aayog's NMPI retains all ten indicators of the Global MPI and incorporates two additional India-specific indicators—Maternal Health under the Health dimension and Bank Account under the Standard of Living dimension.
3. The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) serves as the baseline household micro-data source for computing India's National Multidimensional Poverty Index.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Both the UNDP-OPHI Global MPI and NITI Aayog's NMPI share the exact same three equally weighted dimensions (Health, Education, Standard of Living at 1/3 each). However, NITI Aayog expands the 10 Global indicators to 12 indicators by adding Maternal Health and Bank Account, using National Family Health Survey (NFHS) datasets.

exp.why: NITI Aayog's National MPI does not introduce a fourth dimension. Like the Global MPI developed by UNDP and OPHI, the NMPI comprises exactly three dimensions—Health, Education, and Standard of Living—each carrying an equal weight of one-third (33.33%).

While the Global MPI comprises 10 indicators across the 3 dimensions, NITI Aayog's NMPI comprises 12 indicators. It retains all 10 global indicators and adds 'Maternal Health' (under the Health dimension, making 3 health indicators each weighted at 1/9) and 'Bank Account' (under the Standard of Living dimension, making 7 living standard indicators each weighted at 1/21).

NITI Aayog computes the National MPI using unit-level household data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4 and NFHS-5), conducted by the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

ref: NITI Aayog, National Multidimensional Poverty Index: A Progress Review

stem: With reference to the Alkire-Foster methodology used in computing the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. An individual is identified as multidimensionally poor if their weighted deprivation score across all indicators equals or exceeds the poverty cut-off of 33.33%.
2. The composite MPI value is calculated by multiplying the Headcount Ratio (H) of multidimensionally poor people by the average Intensity of deprivation (A) experienced among those poor people.

3. If an individual who is already classified as multidimensionally poor becomes deprived in one additional indicator, the Headcount Ratio (H) increases while the Intensity of poverty (A) remains unchanged.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Alkire-Foster dual-cutoff method computes the Adjusted Headcount Ratio (MPI = H x A), where H is the incidence of poverty (proportion of population with weighted deprivations >= 1/3) and A is the intensity (average deprivation share among the poor). This satisfies 'dimensional monotonicity': if an already poor person suffers an additional deprivation, H stays constant, but A increases, thereby raising the MPI.

exp.why: Under the Alkire-Foster dual-cutoff method, after applying indicator-specific deprivation cutoffs, each individual's weighted deprivations are summed into a deprivation score (c_i). Anyone with a deprivation score equal to or greater than k = 1/3 (33.33%) is identified as multidimensionally poor.

The MPI value (or Adjusted Headcount Ratio, M0) is the product of two sub-indices: Incidence or Headcount Ratio (H = q/n, the proportion of people identified as multidimensionally poor) and Intensity (A, the average proportion of weighted indicators in which those poor people are deprived), i.e., MPI = H x A.

If a person who is already classified as multidimensionally poor (score >= 33.33%) becomes deprived in an additional indicator, the total number of poor people does not change, so the Headcount Ratio (H) remains completely unchanged. Instead, the average deprivation share among the poor—the Intensity of poverty (A)—increases, which in turn raises the overall MPI (H x A). This property is known as dimensional monotonicity.

ref: UNDP Human Development Report Technical Notes; NITI Aayog NMPI Methodology

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Human Development Index (HDI) and the Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI):
items: Statement-I: The Human Development Index (HDI) aggregates normalized dimension indices for health, education, and standard of living using their geometric mean rather than their arithmetic mean, ensuring that poor performance in one dimension cannot be linearly compensated by high performance in another dimension.
Statement-II: In countries that implement highly progressive social welfare transfers, the Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI) value exceeds the unadjusted HDI value.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Since 2010, the UNDP computes the HDI using the geometric mean of its three dimension indices to eliminate perfect substitutability and penalize uneven development across dimensions. The IHDI discounts each dimension's average value for domestic inequality; thus, IHDI equals HDI only under perfect equality and is strictly lower than HDI whenever any inequality exists.

exp.why: In 2010, the UNDP replaced the arithmetic mean with the geometric mean (the cube root of the product of the Health, Education, and Income dimension indices). Unlike the arithmetic mean, which assumes perfect substitutability among dimensions, the geometric mean penalizes unbalanced achievements, meaning a low score in health or education pulls down the overall HDI much more sharply.

The IHDI accounts for inequality across the population by discounting each dimension's average value using the Atkinson inequality measure (1 - A_x). Because inequality is always non-negative, the IHDI represents the 'actual' level of human development after accounting for inequality, whereas the unadjusted HDI represents the 'potential' human development if achievements were distributed equally. Therefore, IHDI equals HDI only when there is zero inequality and can never exceed the HDI, regardless of progressive welfare transfers.

ref: UNDP Human Development Report Technical Note 1 & 2

stem: In the compilation of monetary aggregates in India by the Reserve Bank of India, why are cash balances held by the Central and State Governments with the RBI and currency held in the vaults of commercial banks excluded from the measure of 'Money Supply with the Public'?

opts.A: Money supply is a stock variable that measures only the purchasing power circulating among the money-holding public sector, thereby excluding balances held within the money-creating sector itself.
opts.B: Money supply is a flow variable measured over a fiscal year, whereas vault cash of banks and government treasury balances represent static capital reserves.
opts.C: Both government cash balances with the RBI and commercial bank vault cash are statutorily earmarked toward the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and therefore cannot enter circulation.
opts.D: They represent non-legal-tender accounting entries until they are counter-signed by the Ministry of Finance for public disbursement.

core: Money supply is a stock variable measured at a specific point in time that captures only the spendable financial assets held by the 'public' (money-holding sector: households, firms, and non-bank institutions). Currency and deposits held by the 'money-creating sector' (the Government, the RBI, and the commercial/cooperative banking system) are excluded to avoid double counting and because money sitting inside the issuing/creating machinery is not in active circulation with the public.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because monetary statistics divide the economy into two analytical categories: the 'money-creating sector' (comprising the Central and State Governments, the RBI, and the banking system) and the 'money-holding sector' or 'public' (comprising households, private business firms, local authorities, and non-banking financial institutions). Money supply is a stock variable representing the total stock of money held by the public at a given point in time; cash lying in commercial bank vaults or government treasuries/RBI accounts has not yet entered circulation with the public. Option (B) is incorrect (Trap T1) because money supply is a stock variable measured at a point in time, not a flow variable measured over a period. Option (C) is incorrect because commercial bank vault cash is NOT counted toward CRR (only balances actively maintained in current accounts with the RBI count toward CRR under Section 42 of the RBI Act, though vault cash is eligible for SLR), and government balances have nothing to do with CRR. Option (D) is incorrect because currency notes in bank vaults are already full legal tender.

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3 (Money and Banking); RBI Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy

stem: With reference to the components of Reserve Money (M0) on the liability side of the Reserve Bank of India's balance sheet, consider the following statements:
items: 1. 'Currency in Circulation' within M0 includes both the currency notes and coins held by the non-banking public and the physical vault cash held by commercial banks.

2. 'Other Deposits with the RBI' consists of the excess reserves maintained by scheduled commercial banks above the statutory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) requirement and the surplus treasury balances of the Central Government.
3. Demand deposits maintained with the RBI by quasi-government financial institutions like NABARD, foreign central banks, and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) form part of Reserve Money (M0).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: From the components (monetary liabilities) side, Reserve Money (M0) = Currency in Circulation (Currency with the Public + Cash in hand with Banks) + Bankers' Deposits with the RBI + Other Deposits with the RBI. While M1 excludes bank vault cash, M0 explicitly includes it because vault cash is a base monetary liability of the central bank capable of supporting multiple deposit expansion.

exp.why: Unlike Narrow Money (M1), which only counts 'Currency with the Public', Reserve Money or High-Powered Money (M0) tracks the entire monetary liability created by the monetary authority. Therefore, 'Currency in Circulation' in M0 equals Currency with the Public PLUS Cash with Banks (vault cash).

Both required CRR balances and excess reserves of scheduled commercial banks are categorized under 'Bankers' Deposits with the RBI', not under 'Other Deposits with the RBI'. Furthermore, deposits of the Central and State Governments with the RBI are excluded from M0 components altogether (Instead, they are netted out against gross RBI credit to the government on the sources/assets side).

'Other Deposits with the RBI' is a specific component of both M0 and M1 that comprises demand deposits held with the RBI by quasi-government and development financial institutions (such as NABARD), foreign central banks, foreign governments, and international financial bodies like the IMF and World Bank.

ref: RBI Working Group on Money Supply (Y.V. Reddy Committee Report); Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the accounting identity of Reserve Money (M0) from the 'Sources' (asset) side of the Reserve Bank of India:
items: 1. An increase in the Net Non-Monetary Liabilities (NNML) of the Reserve Bank of India, such as an expansion in the Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA), directly expands Reserve Money (M0), ceteris paribus.

2. One-rupee notes and coins issued by the Ministry of Finance are excluded from the sources of Reserve Money (M0) because they do not constitute a balance-sheet liability of the Reserve Bank of India.

3. When the Central Government draws down its existing cash balances maintained with the RBI to finance public expenditure without issuing fresh Treasury Bills, Net RBI Credit to the Government remains unchanged.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: From the sources side, Reserve Money (M0) = Net RBI Credit to Government + RBI Credit to Commercial Sector and Banks + Net Foreign Exchange Assets of RBI + Government's Currency Liabilities to the Public MINUS Net Non-Monetary Liabilities (NNML) of the RBI. Consequently, NNML acts as a leakage/deduction from base money creation, whereas Government drawdown of deposits with the RBI increases Net RBI Credit to the Government and expands M0.

exp.why: In the sources-side accounting identity of Reserve Money (M0), Net Non-Monetary Liabilities (NNML) of the RBI—which include paid-up capital, reserve funds, and valuation reserves like the Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA)—are SUBTRACTED from the financial assets of the RBI. Therefore, an isolated increase in NNML contracts (or sterilizes) Reserve Money rather than expanding it.

Although one-rupee notes and coins are issued by the Central Government (Ministry of Finance) under the Coinage Act rather than by the RBI, they are explicitly added as a separate source item titled 'Government's Currency Liabilities to the Public' when computing total Reserve Money (M0).

'Net RBI Credit to the Government' is defined as the RBI's gross claims on the Government (holdings of dated G-Secs, Treasury Bills, and Ways and Means Advances) MINUS the cash balances/deposits maintained by the Government with the RBI. When the Government draws down its cash deposits with the RBI to pay contractors or citizens, the subtracted deposit term falls, which directly INCREASES Net RBI Credit to the Government and injects fresh Reserve Money (M0) into the banking system.

ref: RBI Annual Report (Monetary Policy Operations & Balance Sheet Chapter); Y.V. Reddy Committee on Monetary Aggregates

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the computation of Narrow Money (M1) in India:
items: Statement-I: In the computation of Narrow Money (M1), inter-bank demand deposits held by one commercial bank with another commercial bank are excluded.

Statement-II: The Reserve Bank of India classifies both scheduled commercial banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) as part of the 'money-creating banking sector' and therefore excludes demand deposits held by NBFCs and mutual funds with commercial banks from Narrow Money (M1).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Narrow Money (M1) includes only 'Net' demand deposits of the banking system, meaning inter-bank deposits held by one bank with another are excluded to prevent double counting of liquidity within the money-creating banking sector. However, Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), mutual funds, and insurance companies are classified under the 'money-holding public sector' in monetary aggregates, so their demand deposits with commercial banks ARE included in M1.

exp.why: M1 = Currency with the Public + Net Demand Deposits of the Banking System + Other Deposits with the RBI. The word 'Net' specifically signifies that only non-bank public demand liabilities are counted, while inter-bank deposits held by one commercial or cooperative bank with another are excluded so that claims within the banking system itself are not double-counted.

In RBI's monetary compilation framework, the 'money-creating banking sector' comprises only the Reserve Bank of India and the commercial and cooperative banks that accept chequable demand deposits. Financial institutions outside the banking system—such as NBFCs, mutual funds, insurance corporations (LIC), and development financial institutions—are classified as part of the 'money-holding public'. Consequently, demand deposits maintained by NBFCs and mutual funds with commercial banks ARE included in Net Demand Deposits under M1.

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3; RBI Manual on Financial and Banking Statistics

stem: With reference to the traditional monetary aggregates (M1, M2, M3, and M4) compiled in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. M1 : Currency with the public + Net demand deposits with the banking system + Other deposits with the RBI
2. M2 : M1 + Total deposits with the Post Office Savings Organization (including National Savings Certificates)
3. M3 : M1 + Net time deposits with the commercial and cooperative banking system (excluding all Post Office deposits)
4. M4 : M3 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks only
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Across the traditional monetary aggregates (M1 to M4), M1 and M3 capture pure banking-sector liabilities (Narrow Money and Broad Money respectively) and exclude all post office deposits. M2 adds only 'Post Office Savings Bank deposits' to M1, whereas M4 adds 'Total Post Office deposits (both savings and time deposits, but excluding National Savings Certificates)' to M3.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. M1 (Narrow Money) consists of Currency with the Public (CU) + Net Demand Deposits held by the public in commercial and cooperative banks (DD) + Other Deposits held with the RBI (OD).

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. M2 is an intermediate narrow aggregate defined as M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks ONLY (it does not include Post Office time/recurring deposits, nor does any monetary aggregate include National Savings Certificates).

Pair 3 is correctly matched. M3 (Broad Money) equals M1 + Net Time Deposits with the banking system. M3 captures the aggregate monetary resources of the banking sector and completely excludes all Post Office deposits.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched (interchanged with M2). M4 is defined as M3 + Total deposits with the Post Office Savings Organization (comprising both savings deposits and time deposits with post offices, but explicitly excluding National Savings Certificates).

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3 (Box on M1, M2, M3, M4)

stem: Consider the following monetary aggregates compiled in the Indian economy:
items: 1. M3 (Broad Money)
2. M1 (Narrow Money)
3. M4 (Broadest traditional monetary aggregate)
4. M2 (Intermediate monetary aggregate)
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct sequence of the above monetary aggregates arranged in descending order of their degree of liquidity (from most liquid to least liquid)?
core: As we move from M1 to M4, the quantitative volume (broadness) of the monetary aggregate increases (M1 < M2 < M3 < M4), but the degree of liquidity—defined as the ease and speed with which an asset can be used immediately as a medium of exchange without transaction friction or penalty—steadily decreases (M1 > M2 > M3 > M4).

exp.why: Item 1 (M3) ranks third in liquidity: it adds bank time/fixed deposits to M1, which have a fixed maturity lock-in and cannot be withdrawn by cheque on demand without premature withdrawal friction, making M3 less liquid than both M1 and M2.

Item 2 (M1) is the most liquid aggregate (Rank 1 in descending order of liquidity) because all its components—currency with the public and chequable net demand deposits—serve directly and instantaneously as a medium of exchange with zero conversion friction.

Item 3 (M4) is the least liquid aggregate (Rank 4 in descending order of liquidity). Students must avoid Trap T5 (confusing aggregate size with liquidity): while M4 is the largest in monetary volume, it includes both bank time deposits and post office time deposits, which carry the highest withdrawal friction.

Item 4 (M2) ranks second in liquidity: it adds Post Office Savings Bank deposits to M1. While savings accounts at post offices are relatively liquid compared to fixed time deposits, they involve slightly higher transaction friction than commercial bank chequable current/demand deposits, placing M2 between M1 and M3 (hence sequence 2 - 4 - 1 - 3).

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3 (Money Supply and Liquidity Spectrum)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the seasonal behavior of money supply and the money multiplier in India:
items: Statement-I: During major festive seasons or periods of heightened economic uncertainty, a surge in cash withdrawals by the public causes the money multiplier in the economy to decline even if the Reserve Bank of India keeps policy rates and statutory reserve requirements unchanged.

Statement-II: When the public withdraws physical currency from commercial bank demand deposits, the immediate total stock of High-Powered Money (M0) in the economy remains unchanged at the moment of withdrawal.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: A seasonal rise in the public's currency-deposit ratio (cdr) drains fractional-reserve-supporting liquidity from commercial banks and lowers the money multiplier [(1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)]. While the total stock of M0 remains invariant during a cash withdrawal, it is the shift in the composition of M0 from bank reserves to public currency leakage—not the constancy of M0—that explains the fall in the multiplier.

exp.why: The money multiplier is expressed as m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr), where cdr is the currency-deposit ratio and rdr is the reserve-deposit ratio. Since rdr < 1 under fractional reserve banking, the derivative of m with respect to cdr is negative. During festive seasons or economic uncertainty, households prefer holding more cash relative to bank deposits (rising cdr). This cash leakage drains reserves out of the commercial banking system, curtailing multiple credit creation and causing the money multiplier to decline even if the RBI keeps CRR and policy rates constant.

High-Powered Money (M0) equals Currency with the Public + Vault Cash with Commercial Banks + Bankers' Deposits with the RBI. When a depositor withdraws cash from an ATM or bank branch, 'Currency with the Public' rises by the exact amount that 'Vault Cash / Bankers' Deposits with RBI' falls. Thus, the aggregate stock of M0 remains unchanged at the moment of withdrawal. However, this invariance of total M0 does not explain why the money multiplier falls; the multiplier falls because the composition of M0 shifts from high-leverage bank reserves to zero-leverage currency held by the public.

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3 (Money and Banking); RBI Report on Currency and Finance

stem: With reference to the Reserve-Deposit Ratio (rdr) and the credit creation process in the Indian banking system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The effective Reserve-Deposit Ratio of the banking system encompasses both the statutory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) balances mandated by the Reserve Bank of India and the voluntary excess reserves or vault cash held by commercial banks.

2. The actual realized money multiplier in an economy is determined solely by the central bank's statutory reserve ratio and remains unaffected by the precautionary liquidity preferences of commercial banks.

3. Even if the Reserve Bank of India reduces the Cash Reserve Ratio, the broad money multiplier may fail to rise if commercial banks simultaneously accumulate voluntary excess reserves due to heightened borrower default risk.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The actual realized money multiplier is smaller than the theoretical textbook reciprocal of CRR because the denominator (cdr + rdr) includes both public cash leakage (cdr) and banks' voluntary excess reserves inside rdr. Consequently, commercial bank risk aversion can offset central bank reserve easing.

exp.why: In the behavioral money multiplier equation m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr), the total reserve-deposit ratio (rdr) consists of required statutory reserves (CRR balances kept with the RBI) plus working vault cash and any voluntary excess reserves that commercial banks choose to hold (for example, to meet unexpected withdrawal spikes or park overnight in the Standing Deposit Facility).

Only the theoretical maximum credit multiplier in a simplified model (with zero cash holdings by the public and zero excess reserves by banks) is given purely by 1/CRR. In reality, the realized money multiplier is endogenous to the behavioral preferences of both the public (via cdr) and commercial banks (via voluntary excess reserves in rdr).

If the RBI lowers the statutory CRR to inject liquidity during an economic downturn, but commercial banks perceive high credit default risk among borrowers and choose to hold the freed-up liquidity as voluntary excess reserves (or park it in the RBI's Standing Deposit Facility) rather than extending new loans, the total effective rdr does not fall and the money multiplier fails to expand.

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3; RBI Monetary Policy Report

stem: In the analytical framework of the money multiplier [m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)], where 'cdr' denotes the currency-deposit ratio of the public and 'rdr' denotes the reserve-deposit ratio of commercial banks, under which one of the following structural conditions will the Money Multiplier be exactly equal to 1 regardless of changes in the public's currency-deposit ratio?

opts.A: When the public holds zero physical currency and conducts all transactions exclusively through commercial bank demand deposits under a fractional reserve system.
opts.B: When commercial banks are required to maintain a 100 percent reserve-deposit ratio, functioning purely as safe-deposit custodians without lending out deposits.
opts.C: When the public's currency-deposit ratio becomes numerically equal to the commercial banks' statutory reserve-deposit ratio under fractional reserve banking.
opts.D: When the central bank reduces the statutory Cash Reserve Ratio to zero while commercial banks continue to lend out a major proportion of their deposit liabilities.

core: Under a 100% Reserve Banking system (narrow/full-reserve banking), the reserve-deposit ratio (rdr) equals 1.0. Substituting rdr = 1 into m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr) yields (1 + cdr) / (cdr + 1) = 1 for every possible value of cdr, meaning Broad Money equals High-Powered Money (M3 = M0).

exp.why: Option B is correct because when commercial banks hold 100% reserves against all deposits (rdr = 1.0), they cannot extend loans out of deposit inflows or create secondary derivative deposits. Mathematically, substituting rdr = 1 into the multiplier formula gives m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + 1) = 1, completely independent of the value of cdr. Option A is incorrect because if cdr = 0 and 0 < rdr < 1, then m = 1 / rdr > 1. Option C is incorrect because if cdr = rdr < 1, then m = (1 + cdr) / (2 * cdr), which is strictly greater than 1 whenever cdr < 1. Option D is incorrect because if rdr approaches 0 while cdr > 0, then m = (1 + cdr) / cdr = 1 + (1 / cdr) > 1.

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3; Dornbusch & Fischer Macroeconomics

stem: With reference to the macroeconomic impact of the widespread adoption of account-to-account digital retail payment systems such as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Every retail transaction executed through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) directly expands the stock of High-Powered Money (M0) by creating new digital liabilities on the balance sheet of the Reserve Bank of India.
2. A structural shift by households from holding physical cash to retaining balances in commercial bank accounts for digital retail payments lowers the currency-deposit ratio (cdr) in the economy.

3. Other factors remaining constant, a sustained decline in cash leakage induced by account-to-account digital payments enhances the multiple credit creation capacity of the banking system and raises the broad money multiplier.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Account-to-account digital payments like UPI settle between existing commercial bank deposit accounts without creating new central bank liabilities (M0). By reducing the public's need to withdraw physical cash, UPI lowers the currency-deposit ratio (cdr), keeps reserves inside the banking loop, and raises the money multiplier.

exp.why: UPI is an instant payment routing layer built over IMPS that transfers existing commercial bank deposit balances from the payer's bank account to the payee's bank account. It utilizes commercial bank money, not newly issued central bank money, and therefore does not expand the stock of High-Powered Money (M0) on the RBI's balance sheet.

The currency-deposit ratio is defined as cdr = CU / DD (Currency with the Public divided by Deposits). When households substitute physical cash holdings with demand deposits to conduct daily retail payments via UPI, CU declines relative to DD, structurally lowering the currency-deposit ratio.

When payments occur account-to-account via UPI rather than through physical cash withdrawals, funds remain within the commercial banking system as deposits and interbank reserves. This reduction in cash leakage (lower cdr) allows a given base of High-Powered Money (M0) to support a larger volume of bank credit and deposits, increasing the broad money multiplier m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr).

ref: RBI Concept Note on CBDC & Payment Systems Report; Economic Survey

stem: Consider the following statements comparing the monetary mechanics of Retail Central Bank Digital Currency (e-Rupee-R) and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI):
items: Statement-I: When households convert a substantial portion of their commercial bank demand deposits into Retail e-Rupee (CBDC-R) wallets, the commercial banking system's reserve base and the broad money multiplier expand because the funds remain in digital form.

Statement-II: Unlike balances transferred via the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) which remain deposit liabilities of commercial banks, Retail e-Rupee (CBDC-R) is a direct sovereign liability on the balance sheet of the Reserve Bank of India and forms part of Reserve Money (M0).
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Retail e-Rupee (CBDC-R) is digital sovereign currency (a direct RBI liability included under 'Currency in Circulation' in M0), whereas UPI moves commercial bank deposits. Converting bank demand deposits into Retail e-Rupee wallets drains commercial bank reserves just like an ATM cash withdrawal, causing bank disintermediation and shrinking the money multiplier.

exp.why: In monetary accounting, Retail e-Rupee (CBDC-R) is identical in nature to physical banknotes—it is a non-interest-bearing sovereign currency liability of the RBI held directly by the public in digital wallets. When depositors convert commercial bank demand deposits into Retail e-Rupee wallets, commercial banks must surrender an equivalent amount of their reserve balances with the RBI to acquire the e-Rupee for their customers. While Narrow Money (M1) and total Reserve Money (M0) remain unchanged at the instant of conversion, commercial bank reserves drop and the effective currency-deposit ratio rises, causing bank disintermediation and a contraction in the broad money multiplier.

UPI is a payment interface that transfers commercial bank money (deposit liabilities of commercial banks), whereas Retail e-Rupee is central bank money issued under Section 22 of the RBI Act as legal tender. In the RBI's monetary aggregates, e-Rupee in circulation is recorded directly under 'Currency in Circulation' as a component of Reserve Money (M0).

ref: RBI Concept Note on Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC); RBI Annual Report on Monetary Aggregates

stem: With reference to the Reserve Bank of India's balance sheet, foreign exchange market interventions, and sterilization operations, consider the following statements:
items: 1. An unsterilized purchase of US dollars by the Reserve Bank of India from authorised dealers in the spot market simultaneously increases the Net Foreign Exchange Assets (NFEA) of the RBI and expands the domestic stock of High-Powered Money (M0).

2. When the Reserve Bank of India sterilizes a foreign capital inflow by conducting an Open Market Operation (OMO) sale of Government Securities, the total stock of Reserve Money (M0) remains permanently higher because an expansion in Net Foreign Exchange Assets cannot be offset by changes in domestic credit components.

3. A successful sterilization operation through the sale of Government Securities alters the asset composition of the Reserve Bank of India's balance sheet by raising the share of foreign assets relative to domestic sovereign securities, while shielding Broad Money (M3) from secondary multiplier expansion.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: On the sources side of Reserve Money (M0), M0 equals the sum of Net Foreign Exchange Assets (NFEA) and Net Domestic Assets (principally Net RBI Credit to the Government). Sterilization neutralizes the rupee liquidity injected via forex purchases (+NFEA) by selling Government Securities (-Net RBI Credit to Government), leaving total M0 and M3 unchanged while changing the RBI's asset composition.

exp.why: When the RBI buys US dollars from authorised dealers in the spot market to prevent excessive rupee appreciation, its Net Foreign Exchange Assets (NFEA) increase on the asset side of its balance sheet. To pay for these dollars, the RBI credits the rupee reserve accounts of commercial banks held with it, which directly increases Bankers' Deposits with the RBI on the liability side and expands High-Powered Money (M0).

From the sources side of Reserve Money, M0 = Net RBI Credit to Government + RBI Credit to Commercial Sector + Net Foreign Exchange Assets (NFEA) of RBI + Government's Currency Liabilities to the Public - Net Non-Monetary Liabilities. When the RBI conducts a sterilizing OMO sale of Government Securities (or issues Market Stabilisation Scheme securities and impounds the proceeds), it absorbs rupee reserves from banks and reduces 'Net RBI Credit to the Government' by an amount matching the rise in NFEA, thereby keeping the net stock of M0 unchanged.

In a sterilized intervention, the RBI acquires foreign exchange assets (+NFEA) and surrenders domestic Government Securities (-Net RBI Credit to Government) of equivalent rupee value. Consequently, the asset composition of the RBI's balance sheet shifts toward foreign assets relative to domestic sovereign securities, while the net injection of High-Powered Money (M0) is neutralized, preventing an inflationary multiplier expansion in Broad Money (M3).

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3; RBI Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy

stem: With reference to the New Monetary Aggregates (NM1, NM2, and NM3) compiled by the Reserve Bank of India based on the recommendations of the Y.V. Reddy Working Group (1998), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the traditional monetary aggregates (M2 and M4), the New Monetary Aggregates completely exclude all Post Office savings deposits and account for them separately under Liquidity Aggregates.

2. The intermediate aggregate NM2 distinguishes bank term deposits on a maturity basis by including short-term term deposits of residents with a contractual maturity of up to and including one year (alongside NM1, certificates of deposit issued by banks, and the time liabilities portion of savings deposits), while excluding long-term resident term deposits.

3. While traditional M3 excludes non-depository call and term borrowings of the banking system, NM3 excludes both such non-depository borrowings and non-resident repatriable foreign currency fixed deposits such as FCNR(B) accounts.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Y.V. Reddy Working Group (1998) aligned India's monetary statistics with international standards by removing Post Office deposits from monetary aggregates into Liquidity Aggregates (L1-L3), splitting resident term deposits by maturity (up to 1 year in NM2; over 1 year in NM3), excluding non-resident FCNR(B) deposits from domestic time deposits, and including banks' call/term borrowings from non-depository financial institutions in NM3.

exp.why: Under the older monetary framework, M2 and M4 incorporated Post Office savings bank deposits. The Y.V. Reddy Working Group removed all Post Office deposits from the core monetary aggregates (NM1, NM2, NM3) and placed them in the broader Liquidity Aggregate L1.

To reflect the degree of liquidity across maturity buckets, NM2 includes NM1, the time liabilities portion of savings deposits with the banking system, certificates of deposit issued by banks, and short-term term deposits of residents (with a contractual maturity of up to and including one year), whereas long-term term deposits of residents (maturity over one year) are included in NM3.

While NM3 indeed excludes non-resident repatriable foreign currency fixed deposits (such as FCNR(B) deposits, which are treated as external liabilities netted against foreign assets) to restrict domestic deposits to residents only, NM3 explicitly INCLUDES call and term borrowings raised by the banking system from non-depository financial corporations.

ref: RBI Report of the Working Group on Money Supply: Analytics and Methodology of Compilation (Y.V. Reddy Committee, 1998); RBI Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy

stem: Consider the following pairs regarding the Liquidity Aggregates compiled by the Reserve Bank of India:
items: 1. Liquidity Aggregate L1 : NM3 plus all deposits with Post Office Savings Banks (excluding National Savings Certificates)
2. Liquidity Aggregate L2 : L1 plus public deposits held with Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)
3. Liquidity Aggregate L3 : L2 plus term deposits, certificates of deposit, and term money borrowings of Term Lending and Refinancing Institutions
prompt: Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
core: Beyond the core banking monetary aggregate NM3, the RBI tracks broader economy-wide liquidity in three concentric tiers: L1 adds Post Office deposits (excluding NSC), L2 adds the deposit-like liabilities of All-India Financial Institutions (Term Lending and Refinancing Institutions like NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, EXIM Bank), and L3 adds public deposits of NBFCs.

exp.why: L1 is defined as the new broad money aggregate (NM3) plus all deposits with the Post Office Savings Banks, excluding National Savings Certificates (NSCs).

L2 comprises L1 plus the liabilities of Term Lending Institutions and Refinancing Institutions (specifically term money borrowings, term deposits, and certificates of deposit issued by All-India Financial Institutions). Public deposits of NBFCs are added in L3, not L2.

L3 is the broadest liquidity measure and is calculated by adding the public deposits of Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) to L2. The liabilities of Term Lending and Refinancing Institutions belong to L2.

ref: RBI Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy; NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the process of money and credit creation in the banking system:
items: Statement-I: When a commercial bank sanctions and disburses a new loan to a borrower, the total stock of Broad Money (M3) in the economy expands immediately even without any prior injection of Reserve Money (M0) by the Central Bank.

Statement-II: Under a fractional-reserve banking system, commercial banks disburse loans not by handing over physical vault cash, but by opening or crediting a secondary demand deposit account in the borrower's name against the newly acquired loan asset.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In a modern fractional-reserve banking system, 'loans create deposits': when a bank extends credit, it expands both sides of its balance sheet simultaneously by recording a loan asset and crediting the borrower's demand deposit account (a secondary deposit), which immediately increases Broad Money (M3).

exp.why: Because demand deposits held by the public with commercial banks are a direct component of Narrow Money (M1) and Broad Money (M3), the creation of a new deposit entry upon loan disbursement immediately expands M3 without requiring an upfront creation of physical currency or M0.

Commercial banks do not lend out physical currency notes from their vaults when sanctioning credit; instead, they create a book-entry 'secondary deposit' in the borrower's account that the borrower can spend via cheque or electronic transfer. This exact balance-sheet mechanism explains why M3 rises immediately in Statement-I.

ref: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics Ch. 3 (Money and Banking); RBI Functions and Working

stem: With reference to the statutory basis of currency and bank money in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. One-rupee notes and all metallic coins are issued by the Government of India under the Coinage Act, 2011 and are accounted for as the 'Government's currency liabilities to the public' within Reserve Money (M0).
2. Although one-rupee notes and coins are liabilities of the Government of India rather than the Reserve Bank of India, they are put into circulation only through the Reserve Bank of India.

3. Demand deposits held with scheduled commercial banks and cheques drawn upon them enjoy the status of 'limited legal tender' in India, as they can legally discharge debt obligations up to a statutorily notified ceiling.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While banknotes of Rs. 2 and above are issued by the RBI under Section 22 of the RBI Act, 1934, one-rupee notes and all coins are issued by the Central Government under the Coinage Act, 2011 and distributed by the RBI under Section 38 of the RBI Act; bank demand deposits and cheques, however, are fiduciary money and are not legal tender.

exp.why: Under the Coinage Act, 2011, the Government of India has the sole right to mint coins and issue one-rupee notes (signed by the Finance Secretary). In RBI monetary accounting, these constitute 'Government's currency liabilities to the public' and form part of Reserve Money (M0).
Under Section 38 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Central Government puts rupee coins and one-rupee notes into circulation only through the agency of the Reserve Bank of India.

Demand deposits and cheques are optional or fiduciary money (bank money), not legal tender of any kind—a payee can legally refuse to accept a cheque in settlement of a debt. In contrast, metallic coins issued under the Coinage Act, 2011 are 'limited legal tender' (up to Rs. 1,000 for coins of Re. 1 and above).

ref: Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (Sections 22 & 38); Coinage Act, 2011 (Section 6); NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3

stem: Suppose the public deposits a large volume of high-denomination banknotes into scheduled commercial banks following a currency withdrawal drive, and the banks subsequently place these mobilized notes with the Reserve Bank of India. With reference to the monetary accounting of this process, consider the following statements:
items: 1. At the initial stage when the public deposits currency notes into commercial bank accounts, 'Currency with the Public' declines while aggregate bank deposits rise equivalently, leaving the total stock of Broad Money (M3) unchanged.

2. When commercial banks hand over the collected currency notes to the Reserve Bank of India in exchange for balances in their current accounts with the RBI, both 'Currency in Circulation' and total 'Reserve Money (M0)' contract simultaneously by that exact amount.
3. The large-scale conversion of public cash holdings into bank deposits causes a sharp fall in the currency-deposit ratio alongside a surge in excess reserves within the commercial banking system.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Depositing cash into banks shifts money between two components of M3 (reducing Currency with the Public and raising Bank Deposits equally), while banks returning cash to the RBI for reserve balances shifts money between two liability components of M0 (reducing Currency in Circulation and raising Bankers' Deposits with RBI equally) without automatically shrinking M0 unless drained via outright open market sales or permanent extinguishment.

exp.why: Broad Money (M3) equals Currency with the Public plus Demand Deposits plus Time Deposits plus 'Other' Deposits with RBI. When households deposit cash into bank accounts, Currency with the Public falls and Demand/Time Deposits increase by the identical amount, leaving M3 unchanged at that point.

Reserve Money (M0) comprises Currency in Circulation + Bankers' Deposits with RBI + Other Deposits with RBI. When banks return currency notes to the RBI and receive credit in their RBI accounts, 'Currency in Circulation' falls, but 'Bankers' Deposits with the RBI' increases by the exact same amount. Thus, one liability component of M0 substitutes for another, leaving total M0 unchanged until liquidity is absorbed via non-reserve instruments.

As public cash holdings (C) plummet and bank deposits (D) swell, the currency-deposit ratio (C/D) drops sharply. Simultaneously, because banks cannot immediately lend out the sudden influx of deposits, their cash reserves parked with the RBI surge well above statutory requirements, creating massive excess reserves.

ref: RBI Annual Report 2016-17 (Box on Monetary Impact of Withdrawal of Specified Bank Notes); Economic Survey 2016-17

stem: With reference to the 'Sources of Broad Money (M3)' derived from the consolidated balance sheet of the banking sector in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. 'Net Bank Credit to the Government' is broader than 'Net RBI Credit to the Government', as it includes both the Reserve Bank of India's net credit to the Government and commercial and cooperative banks' investments in Government Securities.

2. When scheduled commercial banks utilize their existing surplus reserves to subscribe to newly issued Central Government dated securities in a primary auction, both 'Net RBI Credit to the Government' and Reserve Money (M0) expand immediately.
3. 'Bank Credit to the Commercial Sector' includes not only loans and advances extended by banks to households and firms, but also banks' investments in commercial paper, shares, and corporate bonds.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: On the asset/source side of Broad Money (M3), 'Net Bank Credit to the Government' sums Net RBI Credit to the Government (a source of M0) and Other Banks' Credit to the Government (commercial/cooperative banks' G-Sec holdings); when commercial banks buy G-Secs using existing reserves, only Other Banks' Credit rises, not M0.

exp.why: In RBI's monetary survey, 'Net Bank Credit to the Government' (a source of M3) consists of two parts: (a) Net RBI Credit to the Central and State Governments, and (b) Commercial and Cooperative Banks' investment in Government Securities (such as Treasury Bills and dated SLR bonds).

When commercial banks buy Government Securities in a primary auction using their existing reserve balances, 'Other Banks' Credit to the Government' increases, NOT 'Net RBI Credit to the Government'. In fact, as banks transfer funds from their RBI accounts into the Central Government's cash balance with the RBI, Bankers' Deposits with RBI fall and Government Deposits with RBI rise, temporarily reducing Net RBI Credit to the Government and contracting M0 until the Government spends the proceeds.

'Bank Credit to the Commercial Sector' in the M3 balance sheet captures all claims of the banking system on the domestic private and public non-government commercial sector, encompassing traditional loans, cash credit, overdrafts, bills purchased/discounted, and banks' non-SLR investments in corporate bonds, debentures, shares, and commercial paper.

ref: RBI Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy (Table on Components and Sources of Money Stock M3); RBI Bulletin Explanatory Notes

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the relationship between money supply, national income, and price levels:
items: Statement-I: A rapid expansion in Broad Money (M3) in a developing economy does not necessarily result in a proportionate rise in the general price level if it is accompanied by a structural decline in the income velocity of money.

Statement-II: As an economy undergoes financial deepening and monetization, households and firms hold a larger proportion of their income in interest-bearing bank deposits as a store of wealth rather than exclusively for immediate transactions, which lowers the rate at which a unit of money turns over to finance nominal GDP.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: By the Fisherian Equation of Exchange (M × V = P × Y), money supply growth exceeding real output growth is non-inflationary to the extent that the income velocity of money (V = Nominal GDP / M3) declines due to financial deepening and rising demand for time deposits as a store of value.

exp.why: According to the quantity identity M × V = P × Y (where M is Broad Money M3, V is the income velocity of money, P is the price level, and Y is real output), an expansion in M3 leads to a proportionate rise in P only if V and Y remain constant. If the income velocity of circulation (V) declines commensurately alongside real output growth, the additional money supply is absorbed as desired money balances without triggering proportionate inflation.

Income velocity of Broad Money is defined as V = Nominal GDP / M3, which is the exact reciprocal of the M3-to-GDP ratio (a standard indicator of financial deepening). As previously unbanked segments enter the formal banking system and households accumulate time deposits as a financial store of wealth or precautionary balance, the M3-to-GDP ratio rises and the velocity of circulation (V) structurally falls. This directly explains why rapid M3 growth during financial deepening need not be inflationary.

ref: RBI Report of the Working Group on Money Supply (Reddy Committee); NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the accounting of payment instruments and credit lines in India's monetary aggregates, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unutilized credit card limits and undrawn sanctioned overdraft facilities are excluded from both Narrow Money (M1) and Broad Money (M3) because they represent contingent credit lines rather than existing monetary liabilities.
2. When a consumer purchases goods using a credit card, the transaction expands the money supply only when the issuing bank settles the payment by crediting the merchant's bank deposit account.

3. Balances loaded by customers into non-bank Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs) are not added separately as an independent component of Broad Money (M3) because the underlying funds are maintained in escrow accounts with scheduled commercial banks.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Monetary aggregates measure actual currency and deposit liabilities of the banking system at a point in time, not unutilized credit limits; furthermore, non-bank digital wallets are backed by commercial bank escrow deposits and are therefore already captured inside bank deposits.

exp.why: Sanctioned but unutilized credit card limits and overdraft facilities are off-balance-sheet loan commitments (potential credit). Money supply (M1 and M3) measures actual deposit and currency liabilities held by the public, so undrawn credit limits are excluded until utilized.

A credit card swipe is the availing of a short-term loan from the card-issuing bank, not a transfer of pre-existing money held by the buyer. The money supply expands when the bank creates a new deposit liability by crediting the merchant's bank account against the loan receivable created on the cardholder.

Under RBI Master Directions on Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs), non-bank PPI issuers are mandated to keep 100% of their outstanding wallet liabilities in an escrow account with a scheduled commercial bank. Since commercial bank deposits are already counted in M1/M3, adding non-bank PPI balances separately would result in double counting.

ref: RBI Master Directions on Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs); RBI Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy

stem: In the compilation of residency-based New Monetary Aggregates (NM1, NM2, and NM3) by the Reserve Bank of India based on the recommendations of the Y.V. Reddy Working Group on Money Supply, why are Non-Resident Foreign Currency Repatriable Fixed Deposits—such as FCNR(B) deposits—excluded from the domestic Broad Money aggregate (NM3), whereas rupee-denominated Non-Resident (NRE and NRO) deposits are included?

opts.A: Commercial banks are statutorily exempt from maintaining Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) on FCNR(B) deposits under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
opts.B: FCNR(B) deposits are guaranteed directly by the Consolidated Fund of India, making them sovereign external debt rather than commercial banking liabilities.
opts.C: Monetary aggregates are designed to capture liquidity that exerts direct transaction and demand pressure on domestic goods and services; foreign-currency repatriable liabilities to non-residents respond primarily to global interest differentials and cannot be used for domestic expenditure without conversion into rupees.
opts.D: Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, commercial banks are prohibited from deploying funds raised through FCNR(B) deposits for domestic lending inside India.

core: Under the Y.V. Reddy Committee residency framework, Non-Resident Foreign Currency Repatriable Fixed Deposits like FCNR(B) are treated as external liabilities (netted against commercial banks' foreign assets) rather than domestic money supply because they are denominated in foreign currency and do not directly represent purchasing power over domestic output.

exp.why: Option C is correct: The Third Working Group on Money Supply (Chaired by Dr. Y.V. Reddy, 1998) aligned India's monetary aggregates with IMF standards by introducing residency criteria. While rupee-denominated non-resident deposits (NRE/NRO) were retained within domestic deposit aggregates due to their direct usability in domestic rupee transactions and statistical integration, repatriable foreign currency deposits held by non-residents [such as FCNR(B)] were excluded from domestic Broad Money (NM3) and classified as external liabilities (netted out while computing Net Foreign Assets of the banking sector) because they bear no exchange risk for the depositor, respond to external interest rate movements, and cannot be spent domestically without currency conversion. Option A is incorrect because FCNR(B) deposits are part of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) and attract CRR/SLR unless specifically exempted for incremental periods. Option B is incorrect as they are commercial bank liabilities, not sovereign debt. Option D is incorrect as banks regularly deploy FCNR(B) funds in domestic rupee credit (via forex swaps) as well as foreign currency loans to residents.

ref: Report of the Working Group on Money Supply: Analytics and Methodology of Compilation (Y.V. Reddy Committee, RBI, 1998)

stem: With reference to the interaction between Central Government cash management and Reserve Money (M0) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. When corporations and households pay direct or indirect taxes to the Union Government through banking channels, it causes an immediate contraction in both systemic banking liquidity and Reserve Money (M0).

2. Under the 'Just-in-Time' fund release framework (such as the SNA-SPARSH mechanism) for Centrally Sponsored Schemes, retaining unspent fiscal balances in the Central Government's account with the RBI rather than in commercial bank accounts keeps Reserve Money (M0) lower until actual expenditure occurs.
3. On the components side of Reserve Money (M0), cash balances held by the Central and State Governments with the Reserve Bank of India are included under 'Other Deposits with the RBI'.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Government deposits held with the RBI are excluded from the components of Reserve Money (M0) and netted out from Gross RBI Credit to the Government on the sources side; consequently, tax collections shift funds out of Bankers' Deposits with the RBI into Government balances, contracting M0, while government spending expands M0.

exp.why: When taxes (such as GST or corporate tax) are paid via banks, the RBI debits 'Bankers' Deposits with the RBI' (which is a component of M0) and credits the Central Government's deposit account with the RBI (which is excluded from M0). On the sources side, higher government deposits reduce 'Net RBI Credit to the Government'. Thus, tax inflows drain systemic liquidity and contract M0 until the government spends the money back into the economy.

Previously, advance release of Centrally Sponsored Scheme funds to Single Nodal Agency (SNA) accounts in commercial banks shifted funds from the Government's RBI account into 'Bankers' Deposits with RBI', artificially expanding M0 and surplus banking liquidity. Under the Just-in-Time (SNA-SPARSH) architecture, funds remain in the Government's account at the RBI until the exact moment of beneficiary payment, keeping M0 and idle banking float lower.

Cash balances and deposits of the Central and State Governments with the RBI are explicitly excluded from 'Other Deposits with the RBI' (and from M0 components altogether), because the Government is treated as part of the money-issuing sector rather than the money-holding public.

ref: RBI Monetary and Credit Information Review; Economic Survey (Monetary Management and Financial Intermediation)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the transmission of High-Powered Money (M0) into Broad Money (M3) and the operation of the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF):
items: 1. If commercial banks face heightened borrower default risk and voluntarily park their surplus liquidity in the Reserve Bank of India's Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) instead of extending new loans, the realized money multiplier declines even if the statutory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) remains unchanged.

2. When commercial banks place overnight surplus funds under the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), the Reserve Bank of India transfers an equivalent value of Central Government securities as collateral to the banks, which simultaneously increases their Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) holdings.

3. During a liquidity trap or period of corporate balance-sheet deleveraging, an open market purchase of government bonds by the central bank guarantees a proportionate expansion in Broad Money (M3) because the money multiplier is strictly determined by statutory reserve requirements.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The money multiplier is an endogenous behavioral ratio that depends on banks' willingness to lend and borrowers' willingness to borrow; when banks hoard excess reserves in the RBI's collateral-free Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), the realized reserve-to-deposit ratio rises and the money multiplier contracts.

exp.why: The money multiplier is given by m = (1 + c) / (c + r_r + r_e), where c is the currency-deposit ratio, r_r is the required reserve ratio (CRR), and r_e is the excess reserve ratio. When banks avoid lending and park surplus liquidity in the RBI's SDF window, r_e rises sharply, reducing the realized money multiplier (M3/M0) even when statutory CRR is constant.

Instituted under Section 17 of the RBI Act, 1934, the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) is an uncollateralized liquidity absorption window. The RBI does not provide any government securities as collateral for funds parked in the SDF, and balances held by banks in the SDF do not qualify as eligible assets for the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).

The money multiplier is not a mechanical constant fixed solely by statutory CRR; it represents an upper ceiling that requires active credit demand and bank lending to materialize. During a liquidity trap or balance-sheet recession, an injection of M0 via Open Market Operations simply accumulates as idle excess reserves or SDF balances with the central bank, causing the money multiplier to fall and preventing a proportionate rise in M3.

ref: RBI Act, 1934 (Section 17); RBI Report on Currency and Finance; NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the long-term structural trends in India's monetary ratios as the economy undergoes formalization and financial development, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Over the long run, wider banking penetration and the institutionalization of saving habits cause the share of Currency with the Public in Broad Money (M3) to exhibit a secular declining trend.

2. A structural decline in the public's currency-to-deposit ratio, combined with a progressive reduction in the statutory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) over decades, exerts a secular upward push on the Broad Money Multiplier.
