stem: With reference to the statutory division of powers between the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Monetary Policy Committee is statutorily empowered to determine both the Policy Repo Rate and the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR).

2. While the Monetary Policy Committee decides the benchmark Policy Repo Rate, the choice and timing of liquidity management tools such as Open Market Operations and Variable Rate Repo auctions rest exclusively with the Reserve Bank of India.

3. Supervisory directives restricting a commercial bank from onboarding new customers or disbursing specific categories of loans are issued by the Reserve Bank of India under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, independent of the Monetary Policy Committee.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, 1934, the MPC's mandate is strictly limited to setting the benchmark Policy Repo Rate, whereas reserve ratios (CRR/SLR), liquidity operations, and regulatory actions under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act belong exclusively to the RBI.

exp.why: Under Section 45ZB(3) of the RBI Act, 1934, the Monetary Policy Committee has the statutory mandate solely to determine the Policy Rate (Repo Rate) required to achieve the inflation target. The power to prescribe the Cash Reserve Ratio (under Section 42 of the RBI Act) and the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act) vests exclusively with the RBI as the central bank, not the MPC.

Once the MPC votes on the Policy Repo Rate, operationalizing monetary policy—including setting the corridor spreads for SDF and MSF, and conducting Open Market Operations (OMOs), Variable Rate Repo (VRR), or Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions—is the exclusive operational prerogative of the RBI.

Prudential regulation and banking supervision are completely distinct from monetary policy rate-setting. When the RBI halts business activities or digital onboarding of a regulated bank for compliance failures, it acts under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, without any involvement of the MPC.

ref: RBI Act, 1934 (Sections 42 & 45ZB); Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (Section 35A)

stem: Consider the following monetary policy operating frameworks adopted by the Reserve Bank of India since independence:
items: 1. Multiple Indicator Approach
2. Credit Planning and Sectoral Allocation Framework
3. Monetary Targeting with Feedback
4. Flexible Inflation Targeting Framework
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the adoption of these frameworks in India, from earliest to latest?
core: India's monetary policy regime evolved sequentially from Credit Planning after bank nationalization (1969–1985), to Monetary Targeting with Feedback (1985–1998), to the Multiple Indicator Approach (1998–2015), and finally to Flexible Inflation Targeting (2016–present).

exp.why: The Multiple Indicator Approach (Item 1) was adopted in April 1998 under RBI Governor Bimal Jalan after financial deregulation rendered broad money (M3) demand unstable; it tracked a wide dashboard of rates, credit, fiscal, trade, and exchange rate indicators until 2015.

The Credit Planning and Sectoral Allocation Framework (Item 2) prevailed from the late 1960s (following the 1969 bank nationalization) until 1985, focusing on directed credit, administered interest rates, and statutory pre-emptions to finance planned development.

Monetary Targeting with Feedback (Item 3) was adopted in 1985 following the Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee Report, using Broad Money (M3) growth as the intermediate target while accommodating real GDP growth and tolerable inflation as feedback.

The Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) Framework (Item 4) was formally adopted in 2016 via the amendment of the RBI Act, 1934 (based on the 2014 Urjit Patel Committee Report), establishing Headline CPI as the nominal anchor (4% +/- 2%). Thus, the chronological sequence is 2 - 3 - 1 - 4.

ref: RBI Report on Currency and Finance; Chakravarty Committee (1985) & Urjit Patel Committee (2014)

stem: When the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) announces an upward revision in the Policy Repo Rate, monetary policy transmission unfolds across financial markets and the real economy through several distinct stages. Consider the following stages:
items: 1. Repricing of short-term money market instruments (such as Treasury Bills and Commercial Papers) alongside commercial banks' External Benchmark Lending Rates (EBLR) and Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rates (MCLR)
2. Near-instantaneous upward shift in the overnight Weighted Average Call Rate (WACR) and Tri-Party Repo (TREPS) rates within the Liquidity Adjustment Facility corridor
3. Narrowing of the positive output gap and gradual moderation in Headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation over a multi-quarter horizon
4. Slowdown in credit-financed private consumption and fixed investment demand in the real economy
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct sequential causal chain from the initial policy rate hike to the final macroeconomic outcome?
core: Monetary transmission proceeds sequentially from the policy rate to the overnight money market target (WACR), then across the term structure of money/bond markets and bank deposit/lending rates (EBLR/MCLR), then to real aggregate demand (consumption/investment), and finally to output gap and inflation with a multi-quarter lag.

exp.why: Stage 2 of transmission (Item 1): Once overnight funding costs rise, arbitrage and expectations transmit the hike along the yield curve to short-term money market instruments (T-Bills, CDs, CPs) and to commercial bank lending rates (automatically for EBLR-linked loans and via marginal funding costs for MCLR-linked loans).

Stage 1 of transmission (Item 2): Because the Policy Repo Rate, SDF, and MSF define the LAF corridor for daily central bank liquidity, an MPC rate hike immediately shifts the overnight inter-bank Weighted Average Call Rate (WACR)—the operating target of monetary policy—and TREPS rates on the very same day.

Stage 4 of transmission (Item 3): As aggregate demand cools relative to potential output, the positive output gap narrows and wage-price pressures subside, moderating Headline CPI inflation with a typical cumulative lag of 2 to 4 quarters. Thus, the exact causal sequence is 2 - 1 - 4 - 3.

Stage 3 of transmission (Item 4): Higher bank lending rates and corporate bond yields increase the cost of borrowing for households and firms, dampening credit-financed durable consumption and private capital expenditure.

ref: RBI Monetary Policy Report; Urjit Patel Committee Report on Monetary Transmission

stem: With reference to the legal distinction between Scheduled Banks and Non-Scheduled Banks in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Only banks included in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 are eligible as of right to obtain normal liquidity accommodation from the Reserve Bank of India at the Bank Rate and through the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), as well as acquire automatic membership of clearing houses.

2. For a bank to be included in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, it must satisfy the Reserve Bank of India that its affairs are not being conducted in a manner detrimental to the interests of its depositors.
3. Unlike Scheduled Commercial Banks, Non-Scheduled Banks are completely exempt from maintaining any statutory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) under Indian banking legislation.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Scheduled Banks listed under the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934 enjoy regular access to the RBI's liquidity windows and clearing houses subject to depositor-protection criteria. However, both Scheduled and Non-Scheduled Banks are statutorily required to maintain Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), though under different statutes and custodial arrangements.

exp.why: Inclusion in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 confers specific statutory privileges on a bank, primarily eligibility to borrow from the RBI under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) and Bank Rate windows for normal operations, alongside automatic membership of clearing houses.

Under Section 42(6)(a) of the RBI Act, 1934, the RBI directs the inclusion of a bank in the Second Schedule only if it fulfills the minimum paid-up capital and reserves requirement and satisfies the RBI that its affairs are not being conducted in a manner detrimental to the interests of its depositors.

Non-Scheduled Banks are not exempt from maintaining a Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR). While Scheduled Banks maintain CRR with the RBI under Section 42(1) of the RBI Act, 1934, Non-Scheduled Banks are mandated under Section 18 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to maintain CRR as well—with the operational difference that Non-Scheduled Banks may hold the required cash reserve in cash with themselves or in a current account with the RBI or its notified agency bank.

ref: RBI Act, 1934 (Section 42); Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (Section 18); RBI Functions and Working

stem: With reference to the regulatory and balance-sheet norms governing Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Small Finance Banks are permitted to accept both demand deposits and time deposits of any tenure, Payments Banks can accept only demand deposits up to a prescribed maximum balance per individual customer.

2. Unlike Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks are strictly prohibited from undertaking any lending activities—including small-ticket micro-loans to Self-Help Groups—and cannot issue credit cards on their own balance sheet.

3. Both Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks must maintain the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) with the Reserve Bank of India, and Payments Banks must additionally invest at least 75% of their demand deposit balances in Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) eligible Government Securities or Treasury Bills with maturity up to one year.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks are differentiated banks designed to deepen financial inclusion, but they operate under fundamentally distinct asset-liability structures. While Small Finance Banks function as full-service niche lenders and deposit-takers, Payments Banks are completely barred from assuming credit risk through lending or credit card issuance.

exp.why: Small Finance Banks can accept all types of deposits (savings, current, fixed, and recurring deposits) without any per-customer regulatory cap, whereas Payments Banks are restricted to accepting only demand deposits (savings and current accounts) up to the RBI-prescribed ceiling (Rs. 2 lakh per individual customer) and cannot accept time deposits.

To insulate depositors from credit risk, RBI guidelines strictly prohibit Payments Banks from undertaking any lending activity whatsoever—even micro-credit to Self-Help Groups—or issuing credit cards (though they may issue debit/ATM cards and act as business correspondents for another bank).

Both categories of differentiated banks are subject to CRR requirements with the RBI. Because Payments Banks cannot lend, they must invest a minimum of 75% of their 'demand deposit balances' in SLR-eligible Government Securities or Treasury Bills with maturity up to one year, and may hold a maximum of 25% in current and time/fixed deposits with other scheduled commercial banks for operational and liquidity management.

ref: RBI Operating Guidelines for Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks

stem: With reference to the prudential and operational norms prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India for Small Finance Banks (SFBs), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Like Local Area Banks, the operational jurisdiction of a Small Finance Bank is geographically restricted to a maximum of three contiguous districts in the State where it is registered.
2. Small Finance Banks are required to maintain a minimum Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 15% of their risk-weighted assets on a continuous basis.
3. To ensure credit granularity, at least 50% of the loan portfolio of a Small Finance Bank must constitute loans and advances of up to Rs. 25 lakh.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Small Finance Banks hold a pan-India banking license rather than the three-district geographical cap applicable to Local Area Banks. Given the inherent credit risks of lending to unserved and small borrowers, the RBI mandates a higher minimum Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 15% and requires at least half of their loan book to consist of small-ticket loans up to Rs. 25 lakh.

exp.why: While Local Area Banks (LABs) are restricted to operating within a maximum of three geographically contiguous districts, Small Finance Banks (SFBs) are granted a pan-India operating license and are not restricted to any three-district geographical boundary.

Because Small Finance Banks primarily cater to small borrowers, micro-enterprises, and unorganized sector entities with higher inherent credit risk profiles, RBI prudential norms require SFBs to maintain a minimum Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 15% of their risk-weighted assets on a continuous basis (with Tier-I capital being at least 7.5%).

To prevent mission drift toward large corporate lending and ensure small-borrower focus, RBI guidelines mandate that at least 50% of the loan portfolio of an SFB must comprise loans and advances of up to Rs. 25 lakh.

ref: RBI Guidelines for Licensing and On-Tap Licensing of Small Finance Banks in the Private Sector; RBI Operating Guidelines for SFBs

stem: With reference to the institutional and regulatory architecture of Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Statutory Shareholding Proportion (Central Government : Sponsor Bank : State Government) : 50 : 35 : 15
2. Overall Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Mandate : 75% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC)
3. Statutory Inspection and Supervision under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 : Respective Sponsor Commercial Bank
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Regional Rural Banks operate under a tripartite equity baseline (50% Central Government, 35% Sponsor Bank, 15% State Government) and a 75% Priority Sector Lending mandate. While the RBI serves as the banking regulator and licensing authority, statutory supervision and inspection of RRBs is conducted by NABARD rather than the Sponsor Bank.

exp.why: Under the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976, the standard issued capital of an RRB is subscribed by the Central Government (50%), the Sponsor Bank (35%), and the concerned State Government (15%). (Following the 2015 Amendment Act, RRBs may also raise capital from other sources provided the combined holding of the Central Government and the Sponsor Bank does not fall below 51%).

Because RRBs are dedicated to rural and agricultural credit delivery, the RBI mandates that RRBs achieve an overall Priority Sector Lending (PSL) target of 75% of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent of Off-Balance Sheet Exposures, whichever is higher.

While the Sponsor Bank provides managerial and financial assistance and the RBI grants banking licenses and prescribes prudential norms under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the statutory power of inspection and supervision over Regional Rural Banks (and Rural Co-operative Banks) under Section 35 of the Banking Regulation Act is vested in NABARD, not the Sponsor Bank.

ref: Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976 (as amended in 2015); RBI Master Direction on Priority Sector Lending

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the regulatory framework for Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) in India:
items: Statement-I: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is empowered to supersede the Board of Directors of an Urban Co-operative Bank for up to five years and permit the bank to raise capital through the issue of equity shares, preference shares, and unsecured debentures within its area of operation.

Statement-II: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 brought the banking, capital adequacy, audit, and board-governance functions of Urban Co-operative Banks directly under the regulatory and reconstructive provisions of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 on par with commercial banks, while leaving only non-banking administrative functions such as incorporation, registration, and election rules with the Registrar of Co-operative Societies.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 resolved longstanding regulatory gaps in Urban Co-operative Banks by extending commercial-bank-style RBI powers over capital issuance, audit, reconstruction, and board supersession to UCBs, while preserving the Registrar of Co-operative Societies' jurisdiction strictly over incorporation, registration, and cooperative election processes.

exp.why: In the interest of depositors and financial stability, the RBI is statutorily empowered to supersede the Board of Directors of an Urban Co-operative Bank (including single-state UCBs) for up to five years and appoint an Administrator. Furthermore, with prior RBI approval, a UCB can issue equity shares, preference shares, or special shares at face value or at a premium, and unsecured debentures or bonds with maturity of not less than ten years to its members or persons residing within its area of operation.

Statement-II explains Statement-I because these exact powers of capital-raising (Section 12), board supersession (Section 36ACA), statutory audit at par with the Companies Act, and compulsory reconstruction/amalgamation without requiring prior moratorium (Section 45) were conferred upon the RBI by the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020, which streamlined dual regulation by confining the State/Central Registrar of Co-operative Societies to administrative incorporation, registration, and management elections.

ref: Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020; RBI Four-Tiered Regulatory Framework for UCBs

stem: With reference to the Reserve Bank of India's framework for Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Reserve Bank of India computes the systemic importance score of banks based on four broad indicators: size, interconnectedness, lack of readily available substitutes or financial institution infrastructure, and complexity.

2. Banks designated as D-SIBs are placed into differentiated buckets and are mandated to maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET-1) capital surcharge over and above the standard Capital Conservation Buffer.

3. Once a commercial bank—whether in the public or private sector—is designated as a D-SIB by the Reserve Bank of India, the Government of India provides an explicit statutory sovereign guarantee covering all its inter-bank and wholesale liabilities.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) are 'Too Big to Fail' institutions whose distress would trigger severe disruption to the real economy. Rather than granting an explicit statutory sovereign guarantee—which would worsen moral hazard—the RBI subjects D-SIBs to bucket-wise additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET-1) capital surcharges to raise their loss-absorption capacity.

exp.why: Aligned with the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) methodology, the RBI calculates a composite systemic importance score for banks in India based on four weighted indicators: size, interconnectedness, substitutability (lack of readily available substitutes or financial institution infrastructure), and complexity.

Based on their systemic importance scores, D-SIBs are allocated into five buckets (Buckets 1 to 5, with Bucket 5 initially kept empty to deter further systemic concentration) and are required to hold additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET-1) capital ranging from 0.20% to 1.00% of Risk-Weighted Assets (RWAs) over and above the Basel III capital conservation buffer.

This statement reverses the causal logic of the D-SIB framework. Designation as a D-SIB does not confer any explicit statutory sovereign guarantee from the Government of India on the bank's inter-bank or wholesale liabilities. On the contrary, because markets perceive such 'Too Big to Fail' banks as enjoying an implicit expectation of government bailout during distress—which creates moral hazard and artificial funding advantages—the RBI imposes stricter additional CET-1 capital surcharges to internalize the negative externality and reduce the probability of failure.

ref: RBI Framework for Dealing with Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs); Basel III Capital Regulations

stem: In the context of macroprudential regulation under the Basel-III framework, suppose the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) increases the regulatory risk weights on commercial banks' unsecured consumer credit and on bank exposures to Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs). Assuming a bank's existing capital base and nominal loan portfolio remain unchanged in the immediate short run, which one of the following will be the direct mechanical impact of this policy action?

opts.A: The bank's total Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA) will expand, lowering its reported Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) and compelling it to either raise fresh capital or moderate lending to those segments.
opts.B: The bank's total Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA) will contract, raising its reported Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) and freeing up surplus Tier-1 capital for priority sector lending.
opts.C: The numerator of the Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) will directly shrink due to mandatory statutory write-downs of unsecured loans, while total Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA) remain constant.
opts.D: The bank's Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) will automatically increase because higher risk weights convert unsecured retail loans into Level-1 High Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA).

core: The Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) equals Total Regulatory Capital (Tier-1 + Tier-2) divided by total Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA). When the central bank increases risk weights on specific credit segments as a macroprudential measure to curb exuberant lending, the denominator (RWA) increases for the same nominal rupee value of loans, thereby reducing the bank's reported CRAR and requiring higher capital allocation per rupee lent.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because CRAR = (Tier-1 Capital + Tier-2 Capital) / Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA). When the RBI hikes risk weights on unsecured personal loans, credit cards, or bank lending to NBFCs (for instance, raising risk weights by 25 percentage points), the mathematical denominator (RWA) inflates immediately for the existing stock and incremental flow of such loans. A larger denominator reduces the reported CRAR (Capital Adequacy Ratio), forcing banks to either infuse more regulatory capital to maintain buffers or raise lending rates and slow credit growth to those riskier segments. Option (B) is incorrect (T3 reverse causation trap) because higher risk weights expand rather than contract RWA and reduce rather than raise CRAR. Option (C) is incorrect because risk-weight adjustments alter the denominator (RWA), not the numerator (existing Tier-1/Tier-2 capital), unless provisioning losses separately erode retained earnings. Option (D) is incorrect because risk weights govern capital adequacy (solvency) and have no role in converting illiquid retail loans into High Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) under the LCR framework.

ref: RBI Master Circular on Basel-III Capital Regulations; Economic Survey Chapter on Monetary Management and Financial Intermediation

stem: With reference to the regulatory capital hierarchy and loss-absorption mechanisms of Scheduled Commercial Banks under the Reserve Bank of India's Basel-III norms, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Additional Tier-1 (AT-1) bonds are perpetual debt instruments with no maturity date, where the issuing bank retains full discretion to skip coupon payments and may exercise a call option only after a minimum statutory period with prior approval of the RBI.

2. Because equity shareholders rank junior to bondholders in the corporate insolvency waterfall, the principal of AT-1 bonds cannot be written down unless the bank's Common Equity Tier-1 (CET-1) capital is first completely wiped out in a formal liquidation proceeding.

3. While Common Equity Tier-1 (CET-1) and Additional Tier-1 (AT-1) constitute 'going-concern' capital designed to absorb losses while the bank remains operational, Tier-2 capital acts as 'gone-concern' capital that absorbs losses when the bank reaches non-viability or winding up.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Basel-III norms, Tier-1 capital (CET-1 + AT-1) serves as 'going-concern' capital capable of absorbing losses to prevent bank insolvency, whereas Tier-2 serves as 'gone-concern' capital. Crucially, AT-1 perpetual bonds carry contractual Point of Non-Viability (PONV) and CET-1 ratio triggers allowing the regulator to permanently write down their principal or convert them into equity to keep the bank alive without entering liquidation or wiping out existing equity shareholders first.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under RBI's Basel-III Master Circular, Additional Tier-1 (AT-1) capital instruments (such as Perpetual Non-Cumulative Preference Shares and Perpetual Debt Instruments) must be perpetual with no fixed maturity date and no step-ups or other incentives to redeem. The issuing bank has full discretion at all times to cancel distributions/coupon payments (which are non-cumulative), and cancellation of coupon does not constitute an event of default. A call option is permissible only after the instrument has run for at least five years and strictly requires prior RBI approval.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While bondholders normally rank above equity holders in traditional corporate liquidation, AT-1 bonds are specialized regulatory 'going-concern' capital governed by RBI's Basel-III guidelines and Section 35A/45 of the Banking Regulation Act. When a bank breaches a pre-specified Common Equity Tier-1 trigger (e.g., CET-1 falling below 6.125%) or reaches the Point of Non-Viability (PONV) as determined by the RBI, AT-1 bonds can be permanently written down in full or converted into equity while the bank is reconstructed as a going concern, without initiating formal liquidation and even without first reducing existing equity share capital to zero (as upheld in the YES Bank AT-1 bond restructuring jurisprudence).

Statement 3 is correct. Basel-III divides total regulatory capital into Tier-1 ('going-concern' capital, comprising CET-1 and AT-1, which absorbs losses on an ongoing basis so that the bank can continue its activities and stay solvent) and Tier-2 ('gone-concern' capital, comprising subordinated debt, undisclosed reserves, and general loss reserves up to prescribed limits, which absorbs losses once the bank ceases to be a going concern or enters liquidation).

ref: RBI Master Circular on Basel-III Capital Regulations; Banking Regulation Act, 1949

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the macroprudential capital buffers prescribed under the Basel-III framework:
items: Statement-I: Unlike the fixed Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB), the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCCyB) is dynamically calibrated using the aggregate credit-to-GDP gap as its main reference indicator to dampen the pro-cyclicality of bank lending.

Statement-II: The Reserve Bank of India activates and raises the Countercyclical Capital Buffer requirement during a severe economic downturn when Non-Performing Assets surge, and lowers it to zero during periods of rapid economic expansion.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Bank lending is inherently pro-cyclical, expanding aggressively during economic booms and contracting sharply during downturns (credit crunch). To counteract this cycle, the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCCyB, ranging from 0% to 2.5% of RWA in Common Equity Tier-1) is built up during periods of excessive credit growth when the credit-to-GDP gap exceeds its long-term trend, and is released during downturns so banks can absorb losses and continue lending to the real economy.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. While the Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB) is maintained at a constant 2.5% of Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA) in the form of Common Equity Tier-1 (CET-1) across normal times so banks can draw it down during stress, the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCCyB) ranges between 0% and 2.5% of RWA. Under RBI's CCCyB framework, the credit-to-GDP gap (the deviation of the credit-to-GDP ratio from its long-term Hodrick-Prescott filtered trend), alongside supplementary indicators like the incremental C-D ratio and GNPA growth, serves as the primary reference guide to mitigate systemic pro-cyclicality.

Statement-II is incorrect because it inverts the macroeconomic cycle logic of the buffer. The RBI activates and builds up the CCCyB (from 0% up to 2.5%) during periods of excessive system-wide credit boom when systemic risks are accumulating (specifically when the credit-to-GDP gap rises above the lower threshold of 3 percentage points, reaching its maximum at 15 percentage points). Conversely, during an economic downturn or recession when credit slows and NPAs materialize, the RBI releases (lowers to zero) the CCCyB so that banks are not forced to deleverage or ration credit to defend high capital ratios.

ref: RBI Guidelines on Implementation of Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCCyB); BIS Basel-III Framework

stem: With reference to the Basel-III Liquidity Standards implemented by the Reserve Bank of India for Scheduled Commercial Banks, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) mandates that a bank must hold an unencumbered stock of High Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) at least equal to its projected total net cash outflows over a 30-calendar-day acute liquidity stress scenario.

2. The entire mandatory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) balance maintained by a commercial bank with the Reserve Bank of India is counted as a Level-1 High Quality Liquid Asset (HQLA) for fulfilling its LCR requirement.

3. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) aims to reduce maturity transformation risk over a one-year horizon by requiring a bank's Available Stable Funding (ASF) to be at least equal to its Required Stable Funding (RSF).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Basel-III complements solvency ratios with two distinct liquidity standards: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) for short-term (30-day) resilience using High Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA), and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) for long-term (1-year) structural funding stability. Statutory CRR balances locked with the RBI cannot be counted as HQLA because they are unavailable for drawdown during a bank-specific stress event unless the RBI lowers the CRR requirement itself.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR = Stock of HQLA / Total Net Cash Outflows over the next 30 calendar days >= 100%) promotes short-term resilience of a bank's liquidity risk profile by ensuring that it has sufficient unencumbered High Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) that can be converted into cash easily and immediately in private markets to survive a severe idiosyncratic and market-wide stress scenario lasting 30 calendar days.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under RBI's LCR guidelines, the required statutory Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) balances maintained with the RBI are NOT counted as Level-1 HQLA, because statutory CRR is impounded for monetary and reserve compliance and is not freely available to the bank to meet immediate liquidity outflows in a stress scenario. Level-1 HQLA includes cash in hand, excess CRR balances held with the RBI above the statutory minimum, excess SLR government securities, and the specific portion of statutory SLR permitted by the RBI under the Facility to Avail Liquidity for Liquidity Coverage Ratio (FALLCR) and Marginal Standing Facility (MSF).

Statement 3 is correct. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR = Available Stable Funding / Required Stable Funding >= 100%) addresses maturity mismatch over a one-year structural horizon. It compels banks to fund their long-term, less-liquid assets (weighted under RSF) with sufficiently stable liabilities such as retail deposits, long-term wholesale borrowings, and regulatory capital (weighted under ASF), preventing excessive reliance on volatile short-term wholesale funding.

ref: RBI Master Circular on Basel-III Framework on Liquidity Standards (LCR and NSFR)

stem: Under the Reserve Bank of India's Prudential Framework for Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning (IRACP), consider the following pairs of stressed asset classifications and their regulatory trigger norms:
items: 1. Special Mention Account-0 (SMA-0) : Principal or interest shows signs of incipient stress with payment overdue between 1 and 30 days
2. Special Mention Account-2 (SMA-2) : Principal or interest payment remains overdue between 61 and 90 days
3. Cash Credit / Overdraft NPA : The account remains 'out of order' for a period of more than 90 days
4. Agricultural Crop Loan NPA : An advance granted for agricultural purposes where interest or principal remains overdue for 180 days irrespective of the crop cycle
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Before a standard loan breaches the 90-day overdue threshold to become a Non-Performing Asset (NPA), banks classify accounts showing early stress into Special Mention Accounts: SMA-0 (1–30 days overdue), SMA-1 (31–60 days overdue), and SMA-2 (61–90 days overdue). However, agricultural crop advances follow an agronomic harvest-linked norm rather than a fixed day-count: two crop seasons past the due date for short-duration crops, and one crop season for long-duration crops.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. For term loans, an account is classified as Special Mention Account-0 (SMA-0) immediately when the principal or interest (or any other amount wholly or partly) remains overdue for a period of 1 to 30 days (with SMA-1 covering 31 to 60 days).

Pair 2 is correctly matched. An account is classified as SMA-2 when the principal or interest payment remains overdue for a period between 61 and 90 days (or for revolving credit facilities like Cash Credit/Overdraft, when the outstanding balance remains continuously in excess of the sanctioned limit or drawing power for 61 to 90 days). If the default persists beyond 90 days, it slips into the Non-Performing Asset (Sub-standard) category.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. In respect of an Overdraft or Cash Credit (OD/CC) account, the facility is classified as an NPA if the account remains 'out of order' for a period of more than 90 days. An account is treated as 'out of order' if the outstanding balance remains continuously in excess of the sanctioned limit/drawing power for 90 days, or if there are no credits continuously for 90 days as on the date of the balance sheet, or if credits are not enough to cover the interest debited during the same period.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. The RBI does not prescribe a uniform 180-day overdue rule for agricultural crop loans. Instead, to align loan repayment with agricultural harvesting cycles, a loan granted for short-duration crops (crops with a crop season of up to one year) is treated as an NPA if the instalment of principal or interest thereon remains overdue for two crop seasons; whereas a loan granted for long-duration crops (crop season longer than one year) is treated as an NPA if the instalment or interest remains overdue for one crop season.

ref: RBI Master Circular on Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning pertaining to Advances (IRACP)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the accounting relationship between Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA), Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR), and Net Non-Performing Assets (NNPA) of a commercial bank:
items: Statement-I: An increase in a commercial bank's Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR) achieved by setting aside higher loss reserves out of its operating profits directly reduces its reported Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) ratio even before any loan recovery or write-off takes place.

Statement-II: A commercial bank can simultaneously report a high Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) ratio and a near-zero Net Non-Performing Assets (NNPA) ratio without having recovered the defaulted loans from borrowers, by maintaining near-100% provisioning against its bad loans.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Gross NPA measures the total book value of defaulted loans before deducting loss provisions, whereas Net NPA equals Gross NPA minus cumulative provisions set aside out of profits. Therefore, raising the Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR) buffers the bank's balance sheet and drives Net NPA toward zero, but does not reduce Gross NPA unless the defaulted loan is actually recovered, upgraded, or written off from the asset book.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. Setting aside loss provisions out of a bank's operating profits increases its Provisioning Coverage Ratio (PCR = Total Provisions / Gross NPAs) and directly reduces its Net Non-Performing Assets (NNPA = Gross NPA minus Provisions). However, mere provisioning does NOT reduce the Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) figure or the GNPA ratio. Gross NPA declines only when the defaulted loan is repaid/recovered in cash, upgraded to a standard asset upon regularization, sold to an Asset Reconstruction Company, or removed from the balance sheet via a technical/prudential write-off.

Statement-II is correct. Because Net NPA is arrived at by deducting accumulated loan-loss provisions from Gross NPA, a bank with substantial operating profits can allocate nearly 100% provisions against its defaulted loans (achieving a very high PCR). Consequently, the bank's Net NPA ratio will drop close to zero—signaling that future balance-sheet shock from those recognized bad loans has already been absorbed by past profits—even while its Gross NPA ratio remains high because the borrowers have not yet repaid the loans.

ref: RBI Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India; IRACP Provisioning Norms

stem: With reference to the resolution and accounting treatment of Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) by Scheduled Commercial Banks in India, consider the following statements regarding 'Technical Write-Offs' and 'Loan Waivers':
items: 1. Once a commercial bank executes a technical write-off on an NPA, it forfeits its legal right to pursue recovery proceedings against the defaulting borrower before Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) or under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

2. Unlike a loan waiver which permanently extinguishes the borrower's debt obligation, a technical write-off is only an internal accounting exercise undertaken by banks to cleanse their balance sheets and achieve tax efficiency.

3. Any subsequent cash recovery realized from a technically written-off loan account is recognized directly as profit in the bank's Profit and Loss account for that financial year, as the bad debt had already been fully provisioned for.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: A technical (or prudential) write-off removes a fully provisioned bad loan from the active asset side of a bank's balance sheet for accounting and tax purposes without extinguishing the borrower's legal liability to repay. By contrast, a loan waiver is an explicit cancellation of debt where the lender surrenders the legal claim to recovery.

exp.why: A technical (or prudential) write-off does not confer any legal relief or debt forgiveness upon the defaulting borrower. The borrower remains legally liable for the principal and accrued interest, and the bank continues to aggressively pursue legal recovery through Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs), the SARFAESI Act, 2002, and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016.

A loan waiver is a policy or commercial decision that legally releases the debtor from the obligation to repay, creating a permanent fiscal or financial loss. Conversely, a technical write-off is only an internal accounting entry at the Head Office level that shifts fully provisioned NPAs off the active balance sheet (into an off-balance-sheet memorandum account) to present cleaner financials and avail tax deductions on bad debt provisions.

Before executing a technical write-off, a bank must make 100% provisioning for the bad loan out of its operating profits. Consequently, when any recovery is subsequently made from that written-off account, the recovered sum flows directly as write-back income into the bank's Profit and Loss (P&L) account, boosting its net profit for that period.

ref: RBI Master Circular on Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning; RBI Financial Stability Reports

stem: With reference to the regulatory framework governing 'Wilful Defaulters', 'Non-Cooperative Borrowers', and 'Fraud Accounts' in the Indian banking system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) norms, any corporate borrower whose loan account remains a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) for more than twelve consecutive months is automatically classified as a 'wilful defaulter' regardless of its cash-flow status.

2. While promoters of entities declared as 'wilful defaulters' remain eligible for institutional credit to establish new commercial ventures, borrowers classified as 'non-cooperative borrowers' face a mandatory five-year statutory debarment from starting new ventures.

3. Because classifying a loan account as 'fraud' is an administrative prerequisite for criminal reporting, commercial banks are legally empowered to classify a borrower's account as fraud unilaterally without issuing a show-cause notice or granting an opportunity of hearing.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: RBI norms strictly distinguish genuine business failure from intentional malfeasance (Wilful Default and Fraud). Following the Supreme Court's landmark ruling in State Bank of India v. Rajesh Agarwal (2023) and RBI's 2024 Master Directions, banks must strictly observe the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem) before classifying either a Wilful Defaulter or a Fraud account.

exp.why: A prolonged NPA does not automatically make a borrower a 'wilful defaulter'. Under RBI's Master Direction on Treatment of Wilful Defaulters (2024), a borrower (with outstanding default of Rs 25 lakh or more) is classified as a wilful defaulter only when intentional default is established through specific criteria: defaulting despite having the capacity to pay, diverting funds for unapproved purposes, siphoning off funds, or disposing of hypothecated/mortgaged security without the lender's knowledge.

The statement reverses the regulatory consequences. It is 'wilful defaulters' (and entities with which their promoters/directors are associated) who are barred from receiving any additional credit facility from banks/NBFCs and face a five-year debarment from institutional finance for floating new ventures after their removal from the wilful defaulter list. Conversely, a 'non-cooperative borrower' is one who withholds necessary information or obstructs asset monitoring, which triggers higher provisioning requirements on fresh credit exposure rather than a five-year ban on new ventures.

In State Bank of India v. Rajesh Agarwal (2023), the Supreme Court held that classifying a borrower's account as 'fraud' entails severe civil consequences—akin to blacklisting the borrower from institutional credit—and therefore the principle of audi alteram partem (right to be heard) must be read into the RBI Master Directions on Fraud. In compliance with this judgment, RBI's revised Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management (July 2024) explicitly mandate issuing a detailed show-cause notice and granting at least 21 days for the borrower to respond before classifying an account as fraud.

ref: Supreme Court Judgment in SBI v. Rajesh Agarwal (2023); RBI Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management (July 2024) & Wilful Defaulters (2024)

stem: With reference to the Reserve Bank of India's revised Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for Scheduled Commercial Banks, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The framework applies to both Public Sector and Private Sector Scheduled Commercial Banks operating in India, while excluding Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks from its ambit.

2. Under the current revised framework, 'Profitability'—measured through a negative Return on Assets (RoA) for two consecutive years—serves as one of the mandatory trigger parameters for placing a commercial bank under PCA.
3. Once a commercial bank breaches Risk Threshold 1 under the PCA framework, mandatory supervisory actions automatically restrict the bank from distributing dividends or remitting profits.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The revised PCA Framework for Scheduled Commercial Banks functions as an early-intervention supervisory tool aimed at restoring the financial health of weak banks before capital is wiped out. In its 2021 revision, the RBI streamlined the trigger metrics from four to three by dropping 'Profitability (RoA)' and retaining only Capital, Asset Quality, and Leverage.

exp.why: The PCA framework applies to all Scheduled Commercial Banks operating in India—including Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, and Foreign Banks operating through branches or subsidiaries—while explicitly excluding Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks.

While negative Return on Assets (RoA) for two, three, and four consecutive years was a trigger parameter under the pre-2021 PCA norms, the RBI explicitly removed 'Profitability (RoA)' as a trigger indicator in the revised PCA framework effective January 2022. Currently, only three parameters are monitored as PCA triggers for banks: (i) Capital (CRAR and CET-1 Ratio), (ii) Asset Quality (Net NPA Ratio), and (iii) Leverage (Basel III Tier-1 Leverage Ratio).

Under the revised PCA menu of mandatory actions, breaching Risk Threshold 1 immediately triggers restrictions on dividend distribution and remittance of profits, alongside requiring promoters, owners, or parent banks (in the case of foreign banks) to infuse capital and reduce leverage. Higher risk thresholds (Thresholds 2 and 3) add restrictions on branch expansion and capital expenditure.

ref: RBI Revised Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for Scheduled Commercial Banks

stem: With reference to the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework introduced by the Reserve Bank of India specifically for Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The PCA framework for NBFCs applies uniformly across all four tiers of the Scale-Based Regulation structure, including Base Layer NBFCs, Standalone Primary Dealers, and Housing Finance Companies.

2. For Core Investment Companies (CICs) covered under the framework, the RBI tracks the exact same set of three risk indicators—CRAR, Tier-1 Capital Ratio, and Net NPA Ratio—as it does for other non-deposit-taking NBFCs.

3. Even at the first supervisory stage (Risk Threshold 1), all NBFCs placed under PCA face mandatory restrictions on dividend distribution and a requirement for promoters to infuse equity, while Core Investment Companies additionally face a restriction on issuing guarantees on behalf of group companies.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: To align regulatory oversight of large NBFCs with commercial banks following systemic defaults in the non-bank sector, the RBI operationalized a tailored PCA framework for NBFCs. It targets Deposit-taking NBFCs and non-deposit-taking NBFCs in the Middle, Upper, and Top Layers (including Government NBFCs from October 2024), while using specialized capital, leverage, and contingent-liability controls for Core Investment Companies.

exp.why: The PCA framework for NBFCs applies only to: (a) all Deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-D) excluding those already exempt, and (b) all Non-Deposit-taking NBFCs (including Core Investment Companies and, since October 2024, Government NBFCs) in the Middle, Upper, and Top Layers. It explicitly excludes NBFCs in the Base Layer (NBFC-BL), NBFCs not accepting/not intending to accept public funds, Primary Dealers, and Housing Finance Companies.

Because Core Investment Companies (CICs) hold stakes primarily in group entities rather than standard retail loan books, the RBI tracks a distinct set of three indicators for CICs under PCA: (i) Adjusted Net Worth to Aggregate Risk Weighted Assets Ratio, (ii) Leverage Ratio, and (iii) Net NPA (NNPA) Ratio. By contrast, for NBFC-Ds and other NBFC-NDs, the tracked indicators are CRAR, Tier-1 Capital Ratio, and NNPA Ratio.

Under the RBI's Menu of Mandatory Actions for the NBFC PCA framework, breaching Risk Threshold 1 immediately subjects all covered NBFCs to restrictions on dividend distribution/remittance of profits and requires promoters/shareholders to infuse equity to reduce leverage. Furthermore, specifically for Core Investment Companies (CICs), Risk Threshold 1 also imposes a mandatory restriction on issuing guarantees or taking on other contingent liabilities on behalf of group companies.

ref: RBI Circular on Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for NBFCs & Extension to Government NBFCs (2024)

stem: With reference to the statutory definition of Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) and their structural differences from Scheduled Commercial Banks in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike commercial banks, NBFCs—including those registered with the Reserve Bank of India as Deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-D)—cannot accept demand deposits, do not form part of the payment and settlement system, and cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves.

2. The statutory deposit insurance cover provided by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) is available only to depositors of banks and does not extend to depositors of Deposit-taking NBFCs.

3. Under the Reserve Bank of India's 'Principal Business' criteria, a non-banking company is statutorily required to register as an NBFC if either its financial assets exceed 50 per cent of its total assets or its income from financial assets exceeds 50 per cent of its gross income, without requiring both conditions to be satisfied simultaneously.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While NBFCs perform financial intermediation akin to banks, they are legally prohibited from creating checkable demand money or directly participating in the core cheque clearing and settlement system. Furthermore, an entity qualifies as an NBFC under Section 45-IA of the RBI Act only when it satisfies both prongs of the cumulative '50-50 Principal Business' test.

exp.why: Even Deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-Ds) can only accept fixed-term public deposits (for a minimum period of 12 months and a maximum of 60 months). They are prohibited from accepting demand deposits (such as savings or current accounts), do not form part of the core payment and settlement system, and cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves.

Under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) Act, 1961, the deposit insurance cover (up to Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank) is strictly limited to commercial banks (including Regional Rural Banks, Small Finance Banks, and Payments Banks) and cooperative banks. Depositors of NBFC-Ds enjoy no DICGC insurance cover.

Under the RBI's '50-50 test' for determining Principal Business under Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934, both conditions are cumulative (AND, not OR). A company is treated as an NBFC only when its financial assets constitute more than 50 per cent of its total assets (netted off by intangible assets) AND income from those financial assets constitutes more than 50 per cent of its gross income.

ref: Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934; RBI FAQ on All You Wanted to Know About NBFCs

stem: Under the Reserve Bank of India's Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework, Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) are categorized into four regulatory tiers—Base Layer (NBFC-BL), Middle Layer (NBFC-ML), Upper Layer (NBFC-UL), and Top Layer (NBFC-TL). In this context, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Peer-to-Peer Lending Platform (NBFC-P2P) and Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA) : Always placed in the Base Layer regardless of asset size
2. Deposit-taking NBFC (NBFC-D) with an asset size below Rs 1,000 crore : Placed in the Base Layer due to sub-threshold asset size
3. Core Investment Company (CIC), Housing Finance Company (HFC), and Infrastructure Finance Company (NBFC-IFC) : Categorized in either the Middle Layer or the Upper Layer, and never in the Base Layer
4. NBFC-Top Layer (NBFC-TL) : Ideally remains empty and is populated only when the RBI perceives a substantial increase in potential systemic risk from specific Upper Layer NBFCs
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: The Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework calibrates the degree of regulatory proportionality to an NBFC's asset size, public deposit access, and systemic interconnectedness. While non-deposit-taking NBFCs below Rs 1,000 crore generally reside in the Base Layer, specific activity categories such as Deposit-taking NBFCs, CICs, HFCs, and IFCs are mandatorily placed in the Middle or Upper Layer irrespective of asset size.

exp.why: Under the SBR framework, NBFC-Peer to Peer Lending Platforms (NBFC-P2P), NBFC-Account Aggregators (NBFC-AA), Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies (NOFHC), and NBFCs not availing public funds and not having any customer interface are always placed in the Base Layer (NBFC-BL), because they do not take balance-sheet credit risk or access public deposits.

The Rs 1,000 crore asset-size threshold for placement in the Base Layer applies only to Non-Deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-ND). Because accepting public deposits carries inherent fiduciary and systemic risks, all Deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-Ds)—irrespective of their asset size—are mandatorily placed in the Middle Layer (or in the Upper Layer if identified by parametric scoring), and never in the Base Layer.

Under the RBI Scale-Based Regulation Master Direction, irrespective of their asset size, Core Investment Companies (CICs), Housing Finance Companies (HFCs), and Infrastructure Finance Companies (NBFC-IFCs) are categorized in either the Middle Layer or the Upper Layer (and never in the Base Layer), while Standalone Primary Dealers (SPDs) and Infrastructure Debt Fund-NBFCs (IDF-NBFCs) always lie in the Middle Layer.

The Top Layer (NBFC-TL) is designed to remain empty under normal financial conditions. It becomes populated only if the RBI is of the opinion that there is an unsustainable or substantial increase in the potential systemic risk spillover from specific NBFCs in the Upper Layer, which are then moved to the Top Layer and subjected to significantly higher capital charges and intensive supervisory scrutiny.

ref: RBI Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Company – Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2023

stem: With reference to specialised Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. An NBFC-Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA) operates strictly as a data-blind fiduciary conduit that facilitates encrypted, consent-based sharing of financial information without storing, viewing, or reselling customer data.

2. An NBFC-Peer-to-Peer (NBFC-P2P) lending platform acts solely as an online intermediary and is prohibited from lending on its own balance sheet, providing credit enhancement, or cross-selling any product other than loan-specific insurance.

3. To help retail lenders diversify default risk, the RBI permits NBFC-P2P platforms to pool funds received from multiple lenders into closed-ended investment schemes offering tenure-linked assured returns.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under RBI's regulatory architecture for specialised NBFCs, both NBFC-Account Aggregators (data fiduciaries) and NBFC-P2P platforms (credit marketplace intermediaries) operate under strict balance-sheet and activity ring-fencing to prevent data monetisation and shadow deposit-taking.

exp.why: Under the RBI Master Direction on NBFC-Account Aggregator (2016), an Account Aggregator retrieves or collects financial information pertaining to a customer from Financial Information Providers (FIPs, such as banks, mutual funds, insurance companies, and GSTN) and consolidates and presents it to Financial Information Users (FIUs) solely based on explicit electronic customer consent. The AA is entirely 'data-blind' as the data travels in an end-to-end encrypted format; the AA cannot view, store, process, or resell the customer's financial data.

Under the RBI Master Direction on NBFC-Peer to Peer Lending Platform (2017, as updated in August 2024), an NBFC-P2P can act only as an intermediary providing an online marketplace to participants involved in peer-to-peer lending. It cannot raise deposits under the Companies Act or RBI Act, cannot lend on its own balance sheet, cannot hold funds on its balance sheet (all fund transfers must occur through bank-managed escrow accounts), cannot provide any credit enhancement or guarantee, and cannot cross-sell any product except for loan-specific insurance.

RBI strictly prohibits NBFC-P2P platforms from pooling lenders' funds into closed-ended schemes or promoting P2P lending as an investment product with features like tenure-linked assured minimum returns or automatic liquidity/replacement options. Each loan on a P2P platform must be matched directly between individual lenders and borrowers following a board-approved pricing policy, and the entire credit risk of default must be borne by the lender without any return assurance from the platform.

ref: RBI Master Directions on NBFC-Account Aggregator (2016) & NBFC-P2P Lending Platform (Updated Aug 2024); Vivek Singh Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the Co-Lending Model (CLM) and the Digital Lending Framework notified by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Co-Lending Model between Scheduled Commercial Banks and NBFCs for Priority Sector Lending, the originating NBFC is required to retain a minimum of 20% share of the individual loans on its own books.

2. Under the Digital Lending Guidelines, all loan servicing, disbursals, and repayments must be executed directly between the borrower's bank account and the Regulated Entity without routing funds through any pool or pass-through account of a Lending Service Provider (LSP).

3. To prevent off-balance-sheet contagion, the RBI completely prohibits Regulated Entities from entering into any First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG) arrangement with FinTech Lending Service Providers.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: RBI's Co-Lending Model combines the low cost of funds of banks with the last-mile reach of NBFCs while mandating 20% risk retention by NBFCs, whereas RBI's Digital Lending and Default Loss Guarantee (DLG) guidelines ring-fence payment flows and allow capped risk-sharing up to 5% of the loan portfolio.

exp.why: Under the RBI's Co-Lending Model (CLM) scheme for Priority Sector Lending, banks are permitted to co-lend with all registered NBFCs (including Housing Finance Companies) based on a prior master agreement. To ensure 'skin in the game' and rigorous credit underwriting by the originating partner, the NBFC is mandatorily required to retain at least 20% share of the individual loans on its books, while the bank takes up to 80% on its books.

To prevent commingling of funds, unauthorised float income, and opacity by unregulated FinTech apps, the RBI's Guidelines on Digital Lending mandate that all loan disbursals and repayments be executed directly between the borrower's bank account and the bank account of the Regulated Entity (Bank/NBFC), without any pass-through or pool account of a third-party Lending Service Provider (LSP).

The RBI does not impose a blanket ban on First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG), formally termed Default Loss Guarantee (DLG). Under the RBI Guidelines on Default Loss Guarantee in Digital Lending (June 2023), Regulated Entities are explicitly permitted to enter into DLG arrangements with Lending Service Providers (LSPs) or other Regulated Entities, provided the total DLG cover does not exceed a statutory cap of 5% of the total loan portfolio and is backed by verifiable collateral in the form of cash deposits, fixed deposits with a lien, or a bank guarantee.

ref: RBI Circular on Co-Lending by Banks and NBFCs (2020); RBI Guidelines on Default Loss Guarantee in Digital Lending (2023)

stem: With reference to the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Once a secured loan account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) and the borrower fails to discharge the liability in full within 60 days of notice, the secured creditor can take possession of the secured asset without the intervention of any court or tribunal.
2. Both State Co-operative Banks and Multi-State Co-operative Banks are legally empowered to invoke the provisions of the SARFAESI Act for the recovery of unpaid secured debts.

3. The provisions of the SARFAESI Act apply to all mortgaged immovable properties, including security interest created in agricultural land and loan accounts where the remaining amount due is less than 20% of the principal and interest.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 empowers banks (including Co-operative Banks) and notified NBFCs to enforce security interests non-judicially after a 60-day default notice post-NPA classification, but Section 31 explicitly exempts agricultural land and loans where less than 20% of principal and interest remains unpaid.

exp.why: Under Section 13(2) and Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, where any borrower makes a default in repayment of a secured debt and their account is classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA), the secured creditor may require the borrower by written notice to discharge the liabilities in full within 60 days. If the borrower fails to do so, the secured creditor can take possession of the secured assets, take over management, or sell/lease the asset to realise the debt without the intervention of any court or tribunal.

In Pandurang Ganpati Chaugule v. Vishwasrao Patil Murgud Sahakari Bank Ltd. (2020), a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld that co-operative banks (both State Co-operative Banks registered under State laws and Multi-State Co-operative Banks) fall within the ambit of 'banking' under Entry 45 of the Union List and qualify as 'banks' under Section 2(1)(c) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, empowering them to recover dues via SARFAESI.

Under Section 31 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, the provisions of the Act specifically do NOT apply to: (a) any security interest created in agricultural land [Section 31(i)]; (b) any case in which the amount due is less than 20% of the principal amount and interest thereon [Section 31(j)]; (c) any financial asset not exceeding Rs. 1 lakh [Section 31(h)]; and (d) a pledge of movables within the meaning of Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

ref: SARFAESI Act, 2002 (Sections 13 & 31); Pandurang Ganpati Chaugule v. Vishwasrao Patil Murgud Sahakari Bank (2020); Ramesh Singh Ch. 12

stem: With reference to India's 'Bad Bank' resolution architecture comprising the National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (NARCL) and the India Debt Resolution Company Ltd (IDRCL), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Public Sector Banks hold a majority equity stake of at least 51% in IDRCL, whereas Private Sector Banks and Financial Institutions hold a majority equity stake of at least 51% in NARCL.
2. NARCL acquires aggregated stressed loan assets from lending banks through a structured consideration of 15% upfront cash and 85% by way of tradable Security Receipts (SRs).

3. The Government of India provides a five-year sovereign guarantee to cover any shortfall between the face value of the Security Receipts issued by NARCL and the actual value realised upon resolution or liquidation.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's Bad Bank employs a public-private principal-agent split: Public Sector Banks hold majority ownership (at least 51%) in NARCL (the asset aggregator and buyer), while Private Sector Banks/FIs hold majority ownership in IDRCL (the operational resolution manager), supported by a 15:85 cash-to-Security-Receipt model with a 5-year sovereign backstop.

exp.why: The shareholding pattern between NARCL and IDRCL is the exact opposite. Public Sector Banks (PSBs) maintain a minimum 51% majority ownership in the National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (NARCL), which is registered with the RBI as an Asset Reconstruction Company under the SARFAESI Act to acquire stressed assets. Conversely, Private Sector Banks and Financial Institutions hold a majority stake (minimum 51%, with PSB ownership capped at 49%) in the India Debt Resolution Company Ltd (IDRCL), which functions as an operational service entity/agent to manage the assets and engage market professionals for turnaround and value realisation.

NARCL acquires fully provisioned legacy stressed assets (typically above Rs. 500 crore across a consortium of lenders) on a 15:85 basis: 15% of the agreed acquisition value is paid upfront in cash to the selling banks, and the remaining 85% is issued in the form of government-guaranteed Security Receipts (SRs).

To enhance the liquidity and credibility of the Security Receipts issued by NARCL, the Union Government approved a sovereign guarantee of up to Rs. 30,600 crore valid for five years. The guarantee can be invoked only after resolution or liquidation of the stressed asset to cover the shortfall between the face value of the Security Receipts and the actual realisation amount.

ref: Department of Financial Services (Ministry of Finance) Framework on NARCL-IDRCL; Indian Economy by Nitin Singhania Ch. 9

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016:
items: Statement-I: While both Financial Creditors and Operational Creditors can initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process upon a default of at least Rs. 1 crore, the Committee of Creditors (CoC) ordinarily comprises only unrelated Financial Creditors with voting power proportional to their financial debt.

Statement-II: Unlike Operational Creditors who supply goods and services on short-term credit, Financial Creditors provide capital for the time value of money under long-term credit agreements and possess the institutional capability to assess the commercial viability and restructuring of the corporate debtor as a going concern.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: As upheld by the Supreme Court in Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India, Financial Creditors exclusively constitute the CoC because they lend capital for the time value of money and possess the technocratic capability to assess long-term corporate viability and restructuring, unlike Operational Creditors whose claims arise from routine trade supplies.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Sections 4, 7, 8, and 9 of the IBC, 2016, both Financial Creditors (banks, bondholders) and Operational Creditors (suppliers of goods and services, employees, government dues) can trigger CIRP if the corporate debtor commits a default of Rs. 1 crore or more. However, under Section 21(2) of the IBC, the Committee of Creditors (CoC) comprises only Financial Creditors (excluding related parties), and Operational Creditors are included in the CoC only in the exceptional circumstance where a corporate debtor has no Financial Creditors at all.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. As outlined by the Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee (BLRC) and upheld by the Supreme Court in Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (2019), the classification between Financial and Operational Creditors for CoC membership is based on an intelligible differentia: Financial Creditors provide large-scale capital for the 'time value of money' after rigorous Techno-Economic Viability (TEV) assessments and are uniquely equipped to evaluate corporate restructuring and haircuts to preserve the debtor as a going concern. Operational Creditors, conversely, supply goods and services on short-term operational credit and are typically uninterested in or unequipped for long-term financial reorganization (though their minimum payout is statutorily protected under Section 30(2)(b) of the Code).

ref: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Sections 7, 9, 21 & 30); Swiss Ribbons Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (2019); Vivek Singh Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following statutory stages under the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016:
items: 1. Constitution of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) and appointment of the regular Resolution Professional
2. Admission of the insolvency application by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and declaration of statutory moratorium under Section 14
3. Public announcement of insolvency and collation of creditor claims by the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP)
4. Verification of the Resolution Applicant's eligibility under Section 29A and approval of the Resolution Plan by a minimum 66% voting share of the CoC
prompt: What is the correct chronological sequence of the above stages from the commencement of the process to the approval of the Resolution Plan?
core: The CIRP follows a strict statutory timeline under the IBC: NCLT admission and Section 14 moratorium initiate the process, followed by the IRP's public announcement and collation of claims, constitution of the CoC to appoint the regular RP, and finally Section 29A vetting and 66% CoC voting before NCLT sanction.

exp.why: Stage 1 is the THIRD step in the sequence (after NCLT admission and claim collation). Under Section 21 of the IBC, only after the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) has collated all claims received against the corporate debtor and determined its financial position does the IRP constitute the Committee of Creditors (CoC). The CoC then holds its first meeting within 7 days of constitution to either confirm the IRP or appoint a new regular Resolution Professional (Section 22). Placing CoC constitution before NCLT admission or claim collation is a chronological error.

Stage 2 is the FIRST step in the sequence. The Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) formally commences on the date the Adjudicating Authority (National Company Law Tribunal - NCLT) admits the insolvency application under Section 7, 9, or 10. Upon admission, the NCLT declares a statutory moratorium under Section 14 (prohibiting institution/continuation of suits or enforcement of security interests against the debtor) and appoints an Interim Resolution Professional (IRP).

Stage 3 is the SECOND step in the sequence. Immediately upon appointment (within 3 days), the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) makes a public announcement of the corporate insolvency resolution process under Sections 13 and 15 calling for the submission of claims by all creditors, and subsequently receives and collates those claims under Section 18.

Stage 4 is the FOURTH step in the sequence. Once the regular Resolution Professional prepares the Information Memorandum and invites Expression of Interest, prospective Resolution Applicants submit plans. Their eligibility is vetted under Section 29A (which bars wilful defaulters, undischarged insolvents, and errant promoters from buying back the company at a haircut), after which the CoC approves the viable Resolution Plan by a vote of not less than 66% of the voting share of Financial Creditors under Section 30(4), followed by final binding sanction by the NCLT under Section 31.

ref: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Sections 13, 14, 18, 21, 22, 29A, 30 & 31); Vivek Singh Ch. 2

stem: Under Section 53 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, consider the following categories of claims to be distributed from the proceeds of the sale of liquidation assets of a corporate debtor:
items: 1. Financial debts owed to unsecured creditors
2. Insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs paid in full
3. Any amount due to the Central Government and the State Government in respect of the whole or any part of the period of two years preceding the liquidation commencement date
4. Wages and any unpaid dues owed to employees other than the workmen for the period of twelve months preceding the liquidation commencement date
5. Debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished security, ranking equally with workmen's dues for the period of twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct descending order of priority ('Waterfall Mechanism') for the distribution of proceeds among the above claims?
core: Section 53 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 establishes a strict statutory 'Waterfall Mechanism' for distributing liquidation proceeds, deliberately subordinating sovereign tax and government dues below both secured creditors and unsecured financial creditors to promote credit market certainty.

exp.why: Under Section 53(1)(d) of the IBC, financial debts owed to unsecured creditors rank fourth in the liquidation waterfall—below employee wages (12 months) but strictly above Central and State Government dues.
Under Section 53(1)(a) of the IBC, the insolvency resolution process costs and the liquidation costs must be paid in full first, taking absolute precedence over all other claims.

Under Section 53(1)(e) of the IBC, amounts due to the Central Government and State Governments (for the preceding two years) rank fifth in the waterfall, pari passu with unpaid dues of a secured creditor following the enforcement of security interest. A common misconception (Trap T5) is placing sovereign dues at the top of the waterfall; the IBC deliberately places Crown debts below even unsecured financial creditors.
Under Section 53(1)(c) of the IBC, wages and any unpaid dues owed to employees other than workmen for the twelve months preceding the liquidation commencement date rank third in the waterfall.

Under Section 53(1)(b) of the IBC, workmen's dues for the twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished security under Section 52 rank equally (pari passu) in the second tier of the waterfall.

ref: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, Section 53(1); Economic Survey on IBC Resolution & Liquidation

stem: With reference to the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) for corporate Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, consider the following statements:
items: 1. An application to initiate a PPIRP against a defaulting MSME can be filed unilaterally either by the corporate debtor itself or by any operational creditor upon a minimum default of ₹10 lakh.

2. Unlike the regular Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) where management vests in the Resolution Professional, the PPIRP follows a 'debtor-in-possession with creditor-in-control' model where the existing Board of Directors or partners continue to manage the corporate debtor.

3. The statutory timeline prescribed for completing the PPIRP is 120 days from the commencement date, comprising 90 days for the submission of the Committee of Creditors-approved resolution plan and 30 days for adjudication by the National Company Law Tribunal.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Introduced via Chapter III-A of the IBC, the Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process (PPIRP) provides a faster, hybrid 'debtor-in-possession with creditor-in-control' resolution track exclusively initiated by an eligible MSME corporate debtor with prior 66% unrelated financial creditor consent.

exp.why: Under Section 54C of the IBC, 2016, ONLY the corporate debtor itself (classified as an MSME with a minimum default of ₹10 lakh) can file an application to initiate PPIRP, and only after obtaining prior approval from its unrelated financial creditors representing at least 66% in value of the financial debt due to them. Neither operational creditors nor financial creditors can unilaterally file a PPIRP application against an MSME.

Under Section 54H of the IBC, during the PPIRP period, the management of the affairs of the corporate debtor continues to vest in the Board of Directors or the partners of the corporate debtor ('debtor-in-possession'), subject to oversight by the Committee of Creditors ('creditor-in-control'), unless the CoC votes (by at least 66% voting share) to vest management in the Resolution Professional due to fraud or gross mismanagement.
