items: Statement-I: A fresh general allocation of Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to India increases India's official Foreign Exchange Reserves without creating any corresponding increase in India's reported external debt or Capital Account liabilities.

Statement-II: Under the IMF's Sixth Edition of the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6) followed by the Reserve Bank of India, any general allocation of SDRs is recorded through a double-entry system as both an official reserve asset and a long-term external liability in the Capital Account.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under the IMF's BPM6 accounting standard implemented by the RBI, a general allocation of SDRs is not recorded as a one-way free grant; instead, it is booked simultaneously as an increase in official reserve assets (SDR holdings) and a matching long-term external liability (SDR allocations) in the Capital/Financial Account and External Debt statistics.

exp.why: Incorrect. While a fresh general SDR allocation by the IMF augments India's official Foreign Exchange Reserves without requiring export surpluses or market borrowings, it simultaneously increases India's reported long-term external debt and Capital Account liabilities by the exact same amount. Under the BPM6 methodology adopted by the RBI and Ministry of Finance (visible, for instance, following the August 2021 general SDR allocation), SDR allocations are classified as long-term external debt liabilities because a member country incurs an unconditional obligation upon liquidation of the SDR Department or withdrawal from the IMF.

Correct. Under the BPM6 double-entry BoP framework, when the IMF allocates new SDRs to a member country, the increase in SDR holdings is recorded as a debit (increase in reserve assets), and a matching contra-entry is recorded as a credit under 'Other Investment / SDR Allocations' in the Capital/Financial Account, representing a long-term external liability.

ref: IMF Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6); Ministry of Finance Status Report on India's External Debt

stem: With reference to outward capital flows under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Any investment by an Indian entity in the equity capital of an unlisted foreign entity is classified as Overseas Direct Investment (ODI), irrespective of the percentage of equity stake acquired.

2. To guard against illicit round-tripping in the Capital Account, an Indian entity is permitted to invest in a foreign entity that has invested or invests back into India only if the structure does not result in more than two layers of subsidiaries.

3. Resident Indian individuals are permitted to make Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) in foreign entities engaged in banking and insurance activities under the automatic route within their Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) ceiling.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022 drew a bright-line distinction between Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) and Overseas Portfolio Investment (OPI), and replaced the archaic case-by-case RBI approval for ODI-FDI structures ('round-tripping') with an objective rule permitting such structures up to a maximum of two layers of subsidiaries (excluding specified regulated financial intermediaries).

exp.why: Correct. Under Rule 2(1)(q) of the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) includes: (i) acquisition of any unlisted equity capital of a foreign entity (regardless of percentage stake or control), (ii) subscription to the Memorandum of Association of a foreign entity, (iii) investment in 10% or more of the paid-up equity capital of a listed foreign entity, or (iv) investment of less than 10% in a listed foreign entity if accompanied by control. Overseas Portfolio Investment (OPI) is restricted to listed foreign securities below 10% without control.

Correct. Under Rule 19(3) of the 2022 Rules, to address round-tripping concerns without stifling legitimate global business structures, no financial commitment by a person resident in India shall be made in a foreign entity that has invested or invests into India (directly or indirectly) resulting in a structure with more than two layers of subsidiaries (with exemptions for regulated banking, insurance, and systemically important NBFC subsidiaries).

Incorrect. Under Schedule III of the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022, a resident individual is strictly prohibited from making Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) in any foreign entity engaged in financial services activity (including banking and insurance). Even for Indian corporate entities, ODI in a foreign financial services entity is subject to strict net-profit and regulatory registration norms, and non-financial Indian entities cannot make ODI in foreign banking or insurance businesses.

ref: Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022 notified by Ministry of Finance & RBI

stem: In the context of open-economy macroeconomics and the Mundell-Fleming 'Impossible Trinity' (Trilemma), consider the following statements regarding Capital Account Convertibility:
items: 1. If an economy with full Capital Account Convertibility and a fixed exchange rate lowers its domestic policy interest rate below global rates, the resulting capital outflow will force the central bank to sell foreign exchange reserves and contract domestic base money until the interest rate reduction is neutralized.

2. During a surge of foreign capital inflows, a central bank that intervenes in the foreign exchange market to prevent currency appreciation can preserve domestic monetary autonomy in the short run only through sterilized intervention, which entails a fiscal or quasi-fiscal interest cost.

3. Maintaining partial Capital Account Convertibility through quantitative ceilings on short-term external debt and resident capital outflows forces the Reserve Bank of India to completely surrender domestic monetary policy independence whenever it intervenes to curb exchange rate volatility.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Mundell-Fleming Impossible Trinity dictates that a nation cannot simultaneously achieve free capital mobility (full Capital Account Convertibility), a fixed/pegged exchange rate, and an independent monetary policy. India navigates an intermediate corner of this trilemma by retaining calibrated capital controls and sterilized forex intervention, preserving flexible inflation targeting alongside managed exchange rate stability.

exp.why: Correct. Under full Capital Account Convertibility and a fixed exchange rate, uncovered interest parity links domestic and foreign interest rates. If the central bank cuts domestic interest rates below world rates, arbitrage triggers immediate capital flight. To defend the fixed exchange rate peg, the central bank must sell foreign currency reserves and absorb domestic currency, contracting the domestic money supply and driving domestic interest rates back up—thereby demonstrating the complete loss of monetary policy autonomy.

Correct. When foreign capital surges in, a central bank buying foreign exchange to prevent domestic currency appreciation injects domestic base money (unsterilized intervention), which would lower domestic interest rates and fuel inflation. To retain monetary autonomy, the central bank must 'sterilize' this liquidity injection by selling domestic Government Securities (OMOs) or absorbing liquidity via the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF). Because domestic interest rates paid on Indian G-Secs/SDF are typically higher than the yields earned on foreign reserve assets (like US Treasury bills), sterilization carries a quasi-fiscal carrying cost.

Incorrect. The exact macroeconomic rationale for India's calibrated, partial Capital Account Convertibility (maintaining macro-prudential ceilings on volatile short-term debt, FPI debt limits, and LRS caps) is that it creates a buffer in the Impossible Trinity. By preventing unrestricted speculative capital mobility, partial capital controls allow the RBI to smooth excessive exchange rate volatility while still retaining independent domestic monetary policy (Flexible Inflation Targeting).

ref: RBI Report on Currency and Finance; Tarapore Committee Reports on Capital Account Convertibility

stem: Consider the following structural milestones in the post-1991 evolution of India's Balance of Payments and currency convertibility architecture:
items: 1. Acceptance of Article VIII obligations of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) establishing full Current Account Convertibility
2. Introduction of the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) instituting a transitional dual exchange rate regime
3. Introduction of the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) by the Reserve Bank of India for resident individuals
4. Enactment of the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) by Parliament to replace FERA with a civil regulatory framework
prompt: What is the correct chronological order of the milestones given above, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: India's external sector liberalization followed a carefully sequenced path recommended by the High-Level Committee on Balance of Payments (C. Rangarajan Committee): transitioning from an artificially pegged rate to a dual exchange rate under LERMS (1992), unifying the exchange rate (1993), achieving full Current Account Convertibility under IMF Article VIII (1994), modernizing the statutory framework via FEMA (1999), and progressively easing resident capital outflows through the LRS (2004).

exp.why: Occurred second in the sequence (August 1994). Following the unification of the exchange rate in March 1993, India formally accepted the obligations of Article VIII of the IMF Articles of Agreement in August 1994, making the Indian Rupee fully convertible on the Current Account by removing restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions.

Occurred first in the sequence (March 1992). Announced in the Union Budget 1992-93 based on the interim recommendations of the C. Rangarajan Committee on Balance of Payments, LERMS introduced a transitional dual exchange rate system (40:60 ratio) where 40% of foreign exchange earnings had to be surrendered at the official RBI rate for essential imports and 60% could be converted at market-determined rates.

Occurred fourth in the sequence (February 2004). As a step toward gradual Capital Account Convertibility for resident individuals, the RBI introduced the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) in February 2004 (initially with a limit of USD 25,000 per financial year, now USD 250,000), allowing residents to remit funds abroad for permissible current and capital account transactions without prior approval.

Occurred third in the sequence (December 1999). Parliament enacted the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) in December 1999 (which came into force on June 1, 2000), replacing the draconian Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA), 1973, and shifting the legal philosophy from 'conservation of foreign exchange with criminal penalties' to 'facilitation of external trade and payments under civil law'.

ref: RBI History of Central Banking in India; Economic Survey External Sector Chapters

stem: With reference to exchange rate regimes and adjustments in the external value of a domestic currency, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Currency devaluation refers to the decline in the external value of a domestic currency driven by autonomous shifts in market demand and supply of foreign exchange under a floating exchange rate system.

2. Under a managed floating exchange rate regime, the central bank intervenes in the foreign exchange market by buying or selling foreign currencies primarily to moderate excessive volatility rather than to defend a pre-announced fixed parity.

3. Other factors remaining constant, a depreciation of the domestic currency increases the domestic-currency cost of imported capital goods while lowering the foreign-currency price of domestic exports.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Devaluation and revaluation are deliberate official policy actions changing the par value of a currency under a fixed or pegged exchange rate regime, whereas depreciation and appreciation reflect market-driven adjustments under a floating regime. India operates a managed floating regime where the RBI intervenes solely to curb disorderly market volatility without targeting a fixed rate.

exp.why: Statement 1 swaps the concepts of devaluation and depreciation. A decline in currency value caused by market demand and supply forces under a flexible/floating regime is called 'currency depreciation'. 'Devaluation' is an official administrative reduction in the par value of a domestic currency undertaken by the government or central bank under a fixed or pegged exchange rate regime.

Statement 2 is correct. Under a managed floating exchange rate regime (also termed a 'dirty float'), the exchange rate is predominantly determined by market forces in the interbank forex market, but the central bank intervenes through spot and forward purchases or sales of foreign currency to smooth out sharp, disruptive fluctuations without committing to any fixed exchange rate target.

Statement 3 is correct. Ceteris paribus, when the domestic currency depreciates (more domestic currency units are required per unit of foreign currency), domestic importers must pay more in local currency for a given dollar price of imported capital goods, while foreign buyers need fewer units of foreign currency to purchase domestically priced exports.

ref: NCERT Class XII Introductory Macroeconomics Ch. 6 (Open Economy Macroeconomics); RBI Functions and Working

stem: With reference to the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) compiled by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), consider the following statements:
items: 1. It is calculated as the weighted geometric average of the bilateral nominal exchange rates of the Indian Rupee against a basket of currencies of India's major trading partners.
2. Unlike the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER), the NEER index is not adjusted for relative price level or inflation differentials between India and its trading partners.
3. Under the RBI's indexation convention, an increase in the NEER index value indicates a nominal appreciation of the Indian Rupee against the trade-weighted currency basket.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: NEER is a summary index measuring the unadjusted weighted geometric average of bilateral nominal exchange rates of the Rupee against a 40-currency basket of trading partners. Expressed as foreign currency per unit of domestic currency relative to a base year (100), a rise in the NEER index signifies nominal appreciation, while a fall signifies nominal depreciation.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The RBI constructs the NEER index (across both 6-currency and 40-currency baskets) as a weighted geometric mean of the bilateral nominal exchange rates of the Indian Rupee vis-a-vis the currencies of partner countries, weighted by their respective shares in India's external trade.

Statement 2 is correct. NEER is purely a nominal measure and does not account for changes in purchasing power or inflation differentials across countries. Adjusting the NEER for the ratio of the domestic price index to the trade-weighted foreign price indices yields the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER).

Statement 3 is correct. In the RBI's methodology, bilateral exchange rates in the NEER/REER indices are indexed as units of foreign currency per unit of the Indian Rupee (with the base year set at 100). Consequently, an increase in the NEER index above 100 indicates that the Rupee fetches more foreign currency on a trade-weighted basis, signifying nominal appreciation.

ref: RBI Bulletin Methodology on 40-Currency NEER and REER Indices; Economic Survey External Sector Chapter

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) and trade competitiveness:
items: Statement-I: A sustained rise in a country's Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) index above the base-year benchmark of 100 signifies a loss in the external price competitiveness of its exports.

Statement-II: The REER index is computed by deflating the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) whenever domestic inflation exceeds foreign inflation, as it multiplies the NEER by the ratio of trading partners' price indices to the domestic price index.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: REER adjusts the NEER for inflation differentials by multiplying NEER (expressed as foreign currency per Rupee) by the ratio of the domestic price level to the trade-weighted foreign price level. When domestic inflation outpaces foreign inflation or the nominal currency strengthens, REER rises above 100, indicating real overvaluation and reduced export competitiveness.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. When the REER index rises above 100, it indicates that the domestic currency has appreciated in real terms relative to the base period—meaning domestic goods have become relatively more expensive compared to foreign goods after accounting for both nominal exchange rate movements and inflation differentials, thereby eroding export price competitiveness.

Statement-II is incorrect because it inverts the price ratio in the REER formula. Since the RBI defines NEER in terms of foreign currency per unit of domestic currency (indirect quotation), REER is calculated by multiplying NEER by the ratio of the domestic price index to the trade-weighted foreign price indices (P_domestic / P_foreign). Therefore, when domestic inflation exceeds foreign inflation, the ratio is greater than 1, which pushes the REER index upward rather than deflating it.

ref: RBI Report on Currency and Finance; NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 6

stem: Suppose during a given fiscal year, the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) of the Indian Rupee depreciates by 3%, while its Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) appreciates by 2% over the same period. With reference to this macroeconomic divergence, consider the following statements:
items: 1. This divergence indicates that the trade-weighted average inflation rate in partner countries exceeded India's domestic inflation rate by more than three percentage points during the period.
2. It implies that India's domestic inflation rate exceeded the trade-weighted average inflation rate of its trading partners by a margin greater than the rate of nominal currency depreciation.
3. Despite the nominal weakness of the Rupee in the foreign exchange market, Indian exporters experience a net erosion in price competitiveness relative to foreign producers.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Percentage change in REER approximately equals percentage change in NEER plus the inflation differential (Domestic Inflation minus Trade-Weighted Foreign Inflation). Consequently, even when a currency depreciates nominally (NEER falls), REER will appreciate if domestic inflation exceeds partner inflation by a margin larger than the nominal depreciation.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. In growth-rate terms, %ΔREER ≈ %ΔNEER + (π_domestic − π_foreign). If partner countries' inflation (π_foreign) had exceeded India's domestic inflation (π_domestic) while NEER fell by 3%, the inflation term (π_domestic − π_foreign) would also be negative, causing REER to depreciate by even more than 3% instead of appreciating by 2%.

Statement 2 is correct. For REER to appreciate by 2% (+2%) while NEER depreciates by 3% (-3%), the inflation differential (π_domestic − π_foreign) must be approximately +5%. Thus, higher domestic inflation in India relative to its trading partners more than offset the 3% nominal depreciation.

Statement 3 is correct. Real trade competitiveness depends on REER rather than nominal exchange rates alone. Because higher domestic inflation raised domestic production prices by roughly 5% relative to foreign competitors while the nominal exchange rate depreciated by only 3%, Indian goods became 2% more expensive in real foreign-currency terms, eroding export competitiveness.

ref: Economic Survey (External Sector); Krugman & Obstfeld, International Economics: Theory and Policy

stem: In international macroeconomic comparisons, the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of developing economies such as India is substantially larger when measured in Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) dollar terms than when converted at market exchange rates. Which one of the following best explains this structural divergence?

opts.A: Productivity differentials between advanced and developing economies are much smaller in non-tradable, labor-intensive service sectors than in tradable goods sectors, keeping domestic prices of non-tradables significantly lower in developing economies.
opts.B: Developing economies maintain partial capital account convertibility and central bank interventions that systematically overvalue their nominal market exchange rates relative to free-market equilibrium.
opts.C: The Purchasing Power Parity computation excludes the valuation of imported intermediate inputs and crude oil while aggregating the final expenditure of developing nations.
opts.D: Market exchange rates are determined exclusively by speculative capital account flows, whereas Purchasing Power Parity rates are derived from central bank foreign exchange reserve ratios.

core: Under the Balassa-Samuelson effect, international productivity gaps are wide in tradable manufacturing sectors (which set economy-wide wage levels) but narrow in non-tradable, labor-intensive services (such as local transport, haircuts, and retail). Lower wages in developing countries make non-tradable services vastly cheaper domestically, giving a unit of local currency much greater domestic purchasing power than reflected in market exchange rates.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct and captures the Balassa-Samuelson effect. Market exchange rates primarily reflect the supply and demand for internationally traded goods, assets, and cross-border services. In developing countries, lower productivity in tradable sectors keeps general nominal wages low compared to advanced economies. However, because productivity in non-tradable, labor-intensive domestic services (like healthcare, local construction, education, and personal services) does not differ as drastically across countries, lower domestic wages translate into much lower domestic prices for non-tradables. Since PPP compares the cost of an entire basket of goods and services (including non-tradables), a developing nation's real output and purchasing power are much higher in PPP terms than at market exchange rates. Option (B) is incorrect because nominal overvaluation would actually make nominal dollar GDP appear artificially higher, not lower. Options (C) and (D) are factually incorrect distortions of national income and PPP methodology.

ref: NCERT Class XII Macroeconomics Ch. 6; IMF World Economic Outlook Methodology on PPP vs Market GDP

stem: With reference to the impact of currency depreciation on a country's trade balance, consider the following statements:
items: 1. According to the Marshall-Lerner condition, a depreciation of the domestic currency improves the trade balance only if the sum of the absolute price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than one.

2. Under the J-Curve effect, a sharp depreciation of the domestic currency immediately narrows the trade deficit in the very short run because pre-existing export and import volume contracts are highly price-inelastic.

3. If an economy's imports consist predominantly of price-inelastic essentials invoiced in US Dollars, a depreciation of the domestic currency against the US Dollar tends to expand its import bill in domestic currency terms in the short run.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Currency depreciation affects the trade balance through two opposing channels: a negative valuation (price) effect that raises the cost of imports, and a positive volume (quantity) effect that boosts export volumes and curbs import volumes. The Marshall-Lerner condition requires combined export and import demand elasticities to exceed unity for the volume effect to dominate, while the J-Curve explains why inelastic short-run trade volumes initially worsen the trade deficit before improving it.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Marshall-Lerner condition states that, starting from balanced trade, a currency depreciation or devaluation will improve the trade balance (net exports) only if the sum of the absolute values of the price elasticity of export demand and the price elasticity of import demand exceeds unity (|e_x| + |e_m| > 1).

Statement 2 is incorrect because it reverses the short-run direction of the J-Curve effect. In the immediate aftermath of a currency depreciation, export and import quantities are bound by pre-existing contracts and sluggish consumer/producer adjustments (low short-run price elasticity). Because import prices in domestic currency terms rise immediately while import and export volumes scarcely change, the trade deficit initially widens (worsens) in the short run before narrowing in the medium-to-long run as volumes adjust, tracing a 'J' shape over time.

Statement 3 is correct. When imports such as crude oil, fertilizers, or essential pharmaceuticals are priced in US Dollars and domestic demand for them is highly price-inelastic in the short run, the physical quantity imported does not fall significantly when the domestic currency depreciates, causing total import expenditure in domestic currency terms (and fails to shrink the dollar import bill) to swell.

ref: RBI Report on Currency and Finance; Paul Krugman, International Economics (Exchange Rates and the Trade Balance)

stem: With reference to exchange rate dynamics and international trade invoicing, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: A broad-based depreciation of the Indian Rupee against the US Dollar often fails to generate a proportionate boost in India's export volumes to non-US trading partners in the short run.

Statement-II: Under the Dominant Currency Paradigm, the overwhelming majority of India's cross-border trade with non-US partners is invoiced in US Dollars with sticky short-run dollar prices, while imported intermediate inputs priced in US Dollars simultaneously become costlier in Rupee terms.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under the Dominant Currency Paradigm (Gopinath et al.), when global trade is predominantly invoiced in US Dollars rather than bilateral currencies, a generalized strengthening of the USD against emerging market currencies raises local-currency import prices across all destinations simultaneously without making an exporter's goods cheaper in the destination market's local currency.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Contrary to textbook Mundell-Fleming assumptions of producer-currency pricing, empirical evidence for India shows that when the Rupee depreciates against the US Dollar (especially during a broad global strengthening of the USD), India's short-run export volumes to non-US destinations do not rise proportionately.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Because over 85% of India's trade is invoiced in US Dollars (Dominant Currency Paradigm) and dollar export prices are sticky in the short run, a weaker Rupee against the Dollar does not automatically lower the landed price faced by buyers in Europe, Asia, or Africa whose currencies are also depreciating against the USD. Moreover, high import intensity of Indian exports means USD-invoiced imported inputs become immediately more expensive in Rupee terms, eroding export competitiveness.

ref: RBI Report on Currency and Finance (External Sector Dynamics); IMF Dominant Currency Paradigm Framework

stem: With reference to the cross-border transmission of global monetary policy to the Indian economy, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Holding domestic policy rates constant, an aggressive hike in the US Federal Reserve policy rate widens the positive nominal yield differential in favor of Indian Government Securities (G-Secs), causing domestic G-Sec yields to fall.
2. Portfolio debt outflows triggered by rising US Treasury yields exert downward pressure on the Indian Rupee in the spot foreign exchange market.
3. A narrowing of the interest rate differential between the Indian Rupee and the US Dollar reduces the forward premium on the US Dollar in the Rupee-Dollar forward market.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Monetary tightening by the US Federal Reserve raises US Treasury yields, which narrows (compresses) the positive interest rate differential between Indian G-Secs and US bonds. This compression triggers Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) debt outflows, depreciates the spot Rupee, pushes domestic G-Sec yields up, and lowers the USD/INR forward premium via Covered Interest Parity.

exp.why: Statement 1 reverses the causal mechanism. Indian G-Sec yields normally trade higher than US Treasury yields (a positive spread). When the US Fed hikes policy rates while the RBI holds rates steady, US Treasury yields rise, which narrows (compresses) the positive yield spread in favor of India. As FPIs sell Indian bonds to move back to safer, higher-yielding US Treasuries, Indian bond prices fall and domestic G-Sec yields rise.

Statement 2 is correct. When FPIs liquidate Rupee-denominated debt securities and repatriate capital by converting Rupees into US Dollars, the demand for US Dollars in the onshore spot market rises, causing the Indian Rupee to depreciate.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Covered Interest Rate Parity, the annualized forward premium of the US Dollar against the Rupee approximately equals the nominal interest rate differential between India and the United States. As US interest rates rise relative to Indian interest rates, the interest rate differential narrows, pulling down the USD/INR forward premium.

ref: RBI Monetary Policy Report; Nitin Singhania Indian Economy Ch. on Balance of Payments and Exchange Rate

stem: With reference to the components of India's Foreign Exchange Reserves as reported by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Foreign Currency Assets (FCA) : Multi-currency foreign sovereign securities and deposits with foreign central banks, valued and expressed in US Dollar terms
2. Gold Reserves : Physical bullion held both in domestic vaults in India and in safe custody abroad with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements
3. Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) : Sovereign hard currency notes issued directly by the International Monetary Fund and stored in the physical vaults of the RBI
4. Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) : Portion of India's mandatory quota contribution to the IMF paid in foreign exchange or SDRs that can be accessed without policy conditionality
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: India's Foreign Exchange Reserves comprise four components: Foreign Currency Assets (FCA, the largest share), Gold, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) in the IMF. SDRs are purely book-entry international reserve assets created by the IMF representing a potential claim on the freely usable currencies of IMF members, not physical currency notes.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Under the RBI Act, 1934, Foreign Currency Assets include holdings in major convertible currencies (USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, etc.) invested in foreign sovereign bonds, treasury bills, and deposits with other central banks and the BIS, all converted and reported in US Dollar terms.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. As disclosed in RBI's half-yearly reports on Management of Foreign Exchange Reserves, the RBI holds physical gold reserves both domestically (in vaults at Mumbai and Nagpur) and in safe custody abroad with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) are neither a currency nor a direct liability/claim on the IMF, and they do not exist as physical currency notes. They are an interest-bearing international reserve asset and unit of account created by the IMF in 1969, held as electronic book entries in the IMF's SDR Department, representing a potential claim on the freely usable currencies of IMF member countries.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. The Reserve Tranche Position is the difference between a member's IMF quota and the IMF's holdings of its domestic currency (initially formed by the up to 25% quota subscription paid in SDRs or freely usable foreign currencies), which the member can draw at any time upon representation of a balance of payments need without IMF policy conditionality.

ref: RBI Half-Yearly Report on Management of Foreign Exchange Reserves; RBI Act, 1934 Section 17 & 33

stem: With reference to the valuation effects on India's Foreign Exchange Reserves, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Even during a week when the Reserve Bank of India conducts zero spot market intervention, the reported US Dollar value of India's Foreign Currency Assets declines if the US Dollar appreciates sharply against the Euro, Pound Sterling, and Japanese Yen.

2. A rise in the secondary market yields of US Treasury securities held in the Reserve Bank of India's portfolio immediately results in a positive mark-to-market capital valuation gain in India's Foreign Exchange Reserves.
3. In India's Balance of Payments (BoP) statement, valuation gains and losses arising from cross-currency exchange rate movements are fully captured as net capital flows under the Capital Account.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Because India's Foreign Currency Assets (FCA) are held in a multi-currency basket (USD, EUR, GBP, JPY) and foreign sovereign bonds but reported in US Dollar terms, headline forex reserves fluctuate due to two valuation effects: cross-currency movements against the USD and mark-to-market bond price changes. Balance of Payments (BoP) statistics strictly exclude such valuation changes.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. While India's Foreign Currency Assets are reported in US Dollar terms, a significant portion is held in non-USD currencies such as the Euro, Pound Sterling, and Japanese Yen. When the US Dollar strengthens against these currencies, the USD-equivalent value of those non-USD holdings shrinks, causing a negative valuation effect on headline reserves even without any dollar sales by the RBI.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Bond prices and bond yields move inversely. When secondary market yields on US Treasury bonds rise, the market price (capital value) of the existing US Treasury securities held in the RBI's portfolio falls, resulting in a mark-to-market valuation loss rather than a gain.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under the IMF's Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6) followed by the RBI, the Balance of Payments records only actual economic transactions and explicitly excludes unrealized valuation changes caused by exchange rate or asset price shifts. Consequently, the change in reserves on a BoP basis differs from the headline change in reserves by the exact magnitude of the valuation effect.

ref: RBI Bulletin: Sources of Accretion to Foreign Exchange Reserves in India; IMF Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6)

stem: With reference to India's quota and Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) in the International Monetary Fund (IMF), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the IMF articles, a member country is required to pay only up to 25 percent of its quota subscription in Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) or widely accepted foreign currencies, while the remainder is paid in its own domestic currency.
2. Drawing upon the Reserve Tranche Position does not constitute a use of IMF credit and is exempt from both IMF economic policy conditionality and periodic service charges.
3. Unlike the Credit Tranche, funds under the Reserve Tranche Position can be drawn only after the IMF Executive Board approves a formal Extended Fund Facility (EFF) arrangement.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: A member country's Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) at the IMF arises from the reserve asset portion (up to 25% paid in SDRs or freely usable foreign currencies) of its quota subscription plus any net IMF use of its domestic currency. Because RTP is the member's own liquid reserve asset rather than IMF credit, it can be drawn unconditionally at any time without fees or an IMF lending program.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Broadly up to 25 percent of a member country's quota subscription must be paid in reserve assets specified by the IMF (SDRs or freely usable foreign currencies like USD, EUR, JPY, GBP, RMB), and the remaining 75 percent is paid in the member's own currency.

Statement 2 is correct. Because the Reserve Tranche Position represents the member's own liquid claim on the IMF, drawing on RTP is not treated as borrowing or using IMF credit; hence, it carries no policy conditionality, no service charge, and no periodic interest charges or fixed repayment schedule.

Statement 3 is incorrect. It confuses the Reserve Tranche with the Upper Credit Tranches. An Extended Fund Facility (EFF) or Stand-By Arrangement (SBA) with Executive Board approval and structural conditionality is required when borrowing under the Credit Tranches beyond a country's RTP. The RTP itself is part of India's headline foreign exchange reserves and can be encashed on demand upon representation of a balance of payments need.

ref: IMF Articles of Agreement (Article III & Article V); Ramesh Singh Indian Economy Ch. on External Sector

stem: With reference to the Reserve Bank of India's foreign exchange intervention and domestic liquidity management, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: When the Reserve Bank of India intervenes in the spot foreign exchange market by selling US Dollars to arrest sharp depreciation of the Rupee, it drains equivalent Rupee liquidity from the domestic banking system and puts upward pressure on overnight call money rates.

Statement-II: To sterilize the domestic liquidity contraction caused by heavy spot US Dollar sales and keep overnight money market rates aligned with the policy repo rate, the Reserve Bank of India conducts outright Open Market Operation (OMO) sales of Government Securities or issues Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS) bonds.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unsterilized spot sales of US Dollars by the RBI reduce both the RBI's net foreign assets and domestic reserve money (Rupee liquidity), tightening overnight money markets. To sterilize (offset) this Rupee liquidity drainage, the RBI must inject Rupees via Open Market Operation (OMO) purchases of G-Secs or Variable Rate Repo (VRR) auctions—not OMO sales or MSS bonds, which are liquidity-absorption tools.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. When the RBI sells US Dollars in the spot market to authorized dealer banks, the banks pay for those dollars in Indian Rupees, which debits their balances with the RBI. This shrinks high-powered reserve money ($M_0$), tightens systemic Rupee liquidity, and pushes the weighted average call rate (WACR) upward toward or above the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) ceiling.

Statement-II is incorrect because it reverses the direction of the sterilization operation. Because spot USD sales absorb Rupee liquidity, sterilizing that contraction requires injecting Rupee liquidity back into the banking system—which the RBI achieves through outright Open Market Operation (OMO) purchases of Government Securities, long-term Variable Rate Repo (VRR) auctions, or USD/INR buy-sell swaps. OMO sales and Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS) bonds are liquidity-draining tools used when the RBI is buying excess dollars during massive capital inflows.

ref: RBI Report on Currency and Finance; Monetary Policy Framework & Liquidity Management Guidelines

stem: When the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) conducts a USD/INR 'Buy-Sell' foreign exchange swap auction with Authorised Dealer (AD) banks, which of the following accurately describes the mechanism and its immediate domestic liquidity impact?

opts.A: The RBI sells US Dollars in the spot market to absorb surplus Rupee liquidity and simultaneously agrees to repurchase the same amount of US Dollars at a specified future date.
opts.B: The RBI purchases Indian Rupees in the spot market against the collateral of Government Securities and reverses the transaction at the prevailing repo rate upon maturity.
opts.C: The RBI enters into an outright forward contract to buy US Dollars at a future date without any immediate exchange of Rupee liquidity in the spot leg.
opts.D: The RBI purchases US Dollars from banks in the spot market, thereby injecting Rupee liquidity into the banking system, with a simultaneous contract to sell back the same amount of US Dollars at a specified future date.

core: In an RBI USD/INR forex swap, the nomenclature ('Buy-Sell' vs 'Sell-Buy') is always defined from the perspective of the RBI's action on the US Dollar in the first (spot) leg and the second (forward) leg respectively. Consequently, a 'Buy-Sell' swap injects domestic Rupee liquidity in the near leg while temporarily augmenting the RBI's spot forex reserves, whereas a 'Sell-Buy' swap absorbs Rupee liquidity in the near leg.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct because in a USD/INR 'Buy-Sell' swap, the RBI buys US Dollars from Authorised Dealer (AD) banks in the first (spot) leg in exchange for Indian Rupees, which immediately injects durable Rupee liquidity into the domestic banking system; simultaneously, the RBI contracts to sell back the exact same quantum of US Dollars to those banks at a pre-agreed forward maturity date. Option (A) is incorrect because it describes a 'Sell-Buy' forex swap, which is used to drain Rupee liquidity and support the Rupee during depreciation pressures. Option (B) confuses a foreign exchange swap with a domestic Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) repo/reverse repo operation involving Government Securities. Option (C) confuses a two-legged forex swap (which combines a spot transaction and an offsetting forward transaction) with a single-leg outright forward transaction.

ref: RBI Monetary Policy & Forex Liquidity Operations Reports; Indian Economy by Ramesh Singh (External Sector)

stem: With reference to the USD/INR forward premium and currency hedging in the Indian foreign exchange market, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Covered Interest Parity (CIP) principle, the USD/INR forward premium primarily reflects the interest rate differential between Indian Rupee debt instruments and US Dollar debt instruments of comparable maturity.
2. A narrowing of the policy interest rate differential between the Reserve Bank of India and the US Federal Reserve tends to compress the annualised USD/INR forward premium.

3. A decline in the USD/INR forward premium directly increases the currency hedging cost for Indian importers and domestic corporates servicing unhedged US Dollar External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Covered Interest Parity dictates that the currency of the country with the higher nominal interest rate trades at a forward discount (meaning the foreign currency with the lower interest rate commands a forward premium equal to the interest rate differential). Because Indian importers and ECB borrowers must purchase US Dollars in the forward market to lock in their future Rupee outflow, the USD/INR forward premium constitutes their direct hedging cost.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. According to the Covered Interest Parity (CIP) condition, in the absence of arbitrage, the forward exchange rate premium of the US Dollar against the Indian Rupee approximates the nominal interest rate differential between Indian money market/sovereign yields and corresponding US Dollar yields, adjusted for currency basis risk.

Statement 2 is correct. Because Indian nominal interest rates have historically been higher than US interest rates, the US Dollar trades at a forward premium against the Rupee. When the US Federal Reserve raises rates or the RBI cuts rates such that the spread between Indian and US interest rates narrows, the annualised USD/INR forward premium falls (compresses).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Indian importers and domestic corporates with US Dollar ECB liabilities have future Dollar payment obligations, which they hedge by buying US Dollars in the forward market. The USD/INR forward premium is the extra price above the spot rate they pay to lock in future Dollars. Therefore, a decline in the USD/INR forward premium lowers (reduces)—rather than increases—the currency hedging cost for importers and ECB borrowers.

ref: RBI Financial Stability Report (Forex Market & Forward Premia); Macroeconomics by Dornbusch & Fischer

stem: With reference to the Non-Deliverable Forward (NDF) market for the Indian Rupee, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In an offshore Rupee NDF contract, there is no physical delivery of the principal amount in Indian Rupees at maturity; instead, the net difference between the contracted forward rate and the fixing spot rate is settled in a freely convertible currency such as the US Dollar.

2. The historical growth of offshore Rupee NDF markets in centres like Singapore, London, and Dubai was driven by capital account restrictions and hedging documentation requirements in the onshore Indian foreign exchange market.

3. Under extant Reserve Bank of India regulations, Indian banks are completely barred from participating in the offshore Rupee NDF market, even through their International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) Banking Units (IBUs).
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) are cash-settled offshore currency derivatives designed for currencies with partial capital account convertibility, settling only the net exchange rate differential in US Dollars. To integrate onshore and offshore price discovery and curb external speculative volatility, the RBI permits Indian banks operating IFSC Banking Units (IBUs) in GIFT City to transact in the offshore INR NDF market.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Unlike a deliverable forward contract where both counterparties exchange the full notional principal of the two currencies at maturity, an NDF contract involves no physical exchange of Indian Rupees. At maturity, the contracted NDF rate is compared against the benchmark onshore spot reference rate, and only the net profit or loss is settled in a hard currency (typically USD).

Statement 2 is correct. Because the Indian Rupee is not fully convertible on the capital account and non-resident entities historically faced tight regulatory norms regarding underlying exposure verification and registration to access onshore derivatives, global investors turned to offshore financial hubs (Singapore, London, Dubai, New York) to hedge or take positions on the Rupee via NDFs.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Following the recommendations of the Task Force on Offshore Rupee Markets (Usha Thorat Committee), the RBI permitted Category-I Authorised Dealer banks in India that operate IFSC Banking Units (IBUs) in GIFT City to participate in the offshore Non-Deliverable Derivative Contracts (NDDC / NDF) market with non-residents and other eligible banks, helping bridge the spread between onshore and offshore Rupee rates.

ref: RBI Report of the Task Force on Offshore Rupee Markets; FEMA (Foreign Exchange Derivative Contracts) Regulations

stem: Consider the following statements regarding sovereign central bank currency swap arrangements:
items: Statement-I: Bilateral currency swap arrangements between central banks, such as the India-Japan Bilateral Swap Arrangement and the SAARC Currency Swap Framework, strengthen external sector resilience without altering bilateral customs tariffs or creating a customs union.

Statement-II: Sovereign central bank swap lines operate strictly as a financial backstop facility to provide short-term foreign exchange or local currency liquidity to address Balance of Payments difficulties at pre-determined terms.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Bilateral central bank currency swap lines (such as the $75 billion India-Japan BSA or the RBI's SAARC Swap Framework) are monetary and Balance of Payments liquidity arrangements between central banks. They act as a second line of defense for foreign exchange reserves and are entirely distinct from trade policy instruments like Free Trade Agreements or customs tariff schedules.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Central bank swap arrangements are monetary cooperation agreements signed between central banks (or finance ministries) to safeguard financial stability; they have no bearing on import duties, HS-code tariff schedules, or customs union obligations between the participating countries.

Statement-II is correct and explains Statement-I. Because a central bank swap line is solely a stand-by liquidity mechanism allowing a central bank to draw foreign currency (such as USD, Euro, or Yen) or local currency in exchange for domestic currency at pre-agreed terms to meet short-term Balance of Payments liquidity shortfalls and calm forex volatility, it functions in the monetary sphere rather than the trade-tariff domain.

ref: RBI Annual Report (International Relations & SAARC Currency Swap Framework); Ministry of Finance Releases on India-Japan BSA

stem: Consider the following pairs of cross-border financial instruments and the primary entity that bears the exchange rate risk in the event of a depreciation of the Indian Rupee against foreign currencies:
items: 1. Masala Bonds issued offshore : Overseas investor
2. Unhedged US Dollar-denominated External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) : Indian borrowing corporate
3. Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) [FCNR(B)] Deposits : Non-Resident Indian (NRI) depositor
4. Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs) prior to equity conversion : Overseas bondholder
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: In cross-border finance, currency depreciation risk is always borne by the party whose cash flow entitlement or liability is denominated in a currency different from its functional home currency. Rupee-denominated liabilities (like Masala Bonds and NRE deposits) shift the Rupee depreciation risk onto the overseas investor/depositor, whereas foreign-currency-denominated liabilities (like USD ECBs, FCCBs, and FCNR(B) deposits) place the Rupee depreciation risk on the Indian borrower or bank.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Masala Bonds are Rupee-denominated bonds issued outside India by Indian entities. Although settlement of subscription and redemption is typically executed in US Dollars at the prevailing market exchange rate, the face value and coupon are fixed in Indian Rupees. Therefore, if the Rupee depreciates, the overseas investor receives fewer US Dollars upon maturity and bears the exchange rate risk.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. In an unhedged US Dollar-denominated External Commercial Borrowing (ECB), the principal and interest obligations are fixed in US Dollars. When the Indian Rupee depreciates, the Indian corporate borrower must expend a larger amount of Rupees to purchase the required US Dollars for debt servicing, thereby bearing the full currency risk.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. FCNR(B) term deposits are maintained in designated foreign currencies (such as USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, CAD, AUD), and both the principal and interest are repaid in that same foreign currency. Consequently, the NRI depositor is completely insulated from Rupee depreciation against that foreign currency, and the exchange rate risk is borne by the Indian bank accepting the deposit (unlike NRE deposits, which are denominated in INR and where the NRI bears the Rupee risk).

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs) are issued in a foreign currency with coupon and principal obligations denominated in that foreign currency until the bondholder exercises the option to convert them into equity. Prior to conversion (or if the option is not exercised), any depreciation of the Rupee increases the Rupee cost of servicing and redeeming the bond for the Indian issuing company, which therefore bears the currency risk.

ref: RBI Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations; Economic Survey (External Debt Chapter)

stem: With reference to the Internationalisation of the Indian Rupee and the Special Rupee Vostro Account (SRVA) mechanism notified by the Reserve Bank of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under this framework, Authorised Dealer (AD) banks in India are permitted to open Special Rupee Vostro Accounts for correspondent banks of partner trading countries to settle cross-border trade transactions denominated and invoiced in Indian Rupees.

2. Surplus Rupee balances held by foreign correspondent banks in Special Rupee Vostro Accounts are permitted to be invested in Indian Government Securities (G-Secs) and Treasury Bills in accordance with extant regulatory guidelines.
3. Unlike a Nostro account, a Special Rupee Vostro Account is an account maintained by an Indian Authorised Dealer bank with an overseas central bank denominated in Special Drawing Rights (SDRs).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A Vostro ('yours') account is a domestic-currency (INR) account held by a domestic bank in India on behalf of a foreign correspondent bank, whereas a Nostro ('ours') account is a foreign-currency account held by an Indian bank with a bank abroad. The RBI's SRVA framework reduces dependence on hard currencies for bilateral trade and allows foreign banks to park surplus Rupee balances in Indian sovereign debt instruments.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under the RBI framework for International Trade Settlement in Indian Rupees (INR), Authorised Dealer (AD) banks in India can open Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVAs) for correspondent banks of partner countries. Indian importers pay INR into these accounts against invoices for imports, and Indian exporters are paid out of the balances in these accounts for exports.

Statement 2 is correct. To make holding Rupees attractive for trading partners with whom India runs a trade deficit, the RBI explicitly permits the surplus Rupee balances accumulated in Special Rupee Vostro Accounts to be used for permissible capital and current account transactions, including investments in Government Treasury Bills and Government Securities (G-Secs), as well as project payments.

Statement 3 is incorrect. A Special Rupee Vostro Account is maintained in India by a foreign correspondent bank with an Indian Authorised Dealer bank and is denominated strictly in Indian Rupees (INR), not in SDRs with an overseas central bank. Conversely, an account maintained by an Indian bank with a foreign bank abroad in foreign currency is known as a Nostro account.

ref: RBI Circular on International Trade Settlement in Indian Rupees (INR) & RBI Inter-Departmental Group Report on Internationalisation of INR

stem: With reference to the 'Impossible Trinity' (Mundell-Fleming Trilemma) in open-economy macroeconomics and India's external sector management, consider the following statements:
items: 1. If a central bank prioritizes an independent monetary policy to target domestic inflation while permitting free cross-border capital mobility, it cannot simultaneously maintain a rigid fixed exchange rate.

2. India navigates the trilemma by combining a flexible inflation-targeting monetary policy framework, a market-determined exchange rate with central bank intervention mainly to curb excessive volatility, and calibrated capital account controls.

3. An economy with completely unrestricted capital mobility can indefinitely maintain both a fixed exchange rate peg and a domestic interest rate significantly below global interest rates without depleting its foreign exchange reserves.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Mundell-Fleming Trilemma dictates that an economy cannot simultaneously achieve a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility, and an independent monetary policy. India manages this trade-off through an intermediate regime featuring flexible inflation targeting, a managed float against volatility, and partial capital account convertibility.

exp.why: Under the Mundell-Fleming Trilemma, only two of the three policy goals (fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility, and monetary policy autonomy) can be sustained simultaneously. If a central bank sets domestic interest rates independently and allows free cross-border capital flows, interest rate differentials will trigger capital inflows or outflows that move the nominal exchange rate.

Rather than choosing rigid corner solutions, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) operates a calibrated 'middle ground': it conducts independent monetary policy under the statutory Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework, allows the Rupee to be largely market-determined while intervening smoothly to curb disruptive volatility, and maintains macro-prudential limits on volatile capital flows.

If capital mobility is completely unrestricted and the central bank holds domestic interest rates below global rates, arbitrage induces sustained capital flight out of the domestic currency. To defend a rigid fixed exchange rate peg against depreciation, the central bank must continuously sell foreign exchange reserves and buy domestic currency, rapidly depleting its forex reserves and shrinking the domestic money supply.

ref: RBI Report on Currency and Finance; Krugman & Obstfeld International Economics Ch. 17

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the impact of nominal depreciation of the Indian Rupee against the US Dollar:
items: Statement-I: A depreciation of the Indian Rupee against the US Dollar unambiguously increases the local-currency realization of domestic households receiving fixed-dollar inward remittances from overseas workers, whereas its net benefit to Indian merchandise exporters varies substantially across sectors.

Statement-II: Merchandise export sectors with high import intensity, such as cut and polished diamonds or electronics assembly, realize a larger net gain in operating margins from Rupee depreciation than agricultural or textile exporters with predominantly domestic value addition.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Rupee depreciation directly boosts the Rupee value of inward foreign currency remittances (which require no imported intermediate inputs), its net benefit to merchandise exporters depends inversely on the import intensity of their production.

exp.why: Inward workers' remittances denominated in US Dollars are pure unilateral transfers with zero imported input cost; hence, Rupee depreciation converts each remitted dollar into more Rupees for recipient households. By contrast, merchandise exporters experience varying net benefits depending on their reliance on imported raw materials and components.

Export sectors with high import intensity—such as cut and polished diamonds (which rely on imported rough diamonds), petroleum refining, and electronics assembly—face a simultaneous rise in the Rupee cost of their imported inputs when the Rupee depreciates. This higher input cost neutralizes much of their export revenue gain in Rupee terms, whereas sectors with high domestic value addition (such as agriculture, plantations, and cotton textiles) capture a much larger net margin expansion.

ref: Economic Survey External Sector Chapter; NCERT Introductory Macroeconomics Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the 'Dutch Disease' phenomenon and Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) dynamics in an open economy, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The 'Dutch Disease' refers to a macroeconomic condition in which a massive foreign exchange windfall from a booming natural resource sector causes a sharp real depreciation of the domestic currency.

2. Under the 'spending effect' of a foreign exchange windfall, higher domestic income lowers the prices of domestic non-tradable services relative to internationally tradable manufactured goods, drawing labour and capital into traditional manufacturing.

3. When a central bank intervenes in the foreign exchange market by purchasing foreign currency to prevent nominal exchange rate appreciation without sterilizing the intervention, the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) declines due to a contraction in domestic inflation.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Dutch Disease describes how a surge in foreign currency inflows (from natural resource exports, foreign capital, or remittances) triggers real exchange rate appreciation via the spending and resource-movement effects, eroding the competitiveness of traditional tradable manufacturing sectors.

exp.why: The 'Dutch Disease' arises when a massive foreign exchange windfall (from a resource boom or heavy foreign inflows) causes a sharp real appreciation (not depreciation) of the domestic currency, making the country's traditional manufacturing and agricultural exports uncompetitive in global markets and making imports artificially cheaper.

Under the 'spending effect', windfall income expands domestic aggregate demand. Because the prices of tradable manufactured goods are anchored by global competition, the increased domestic spending bids up the prices of domestic non-tradable goods and services (such as construction, real estate, and local services). This real appreciation pulls labour and capital away from tradable manufacturing into the non-tradable and booming resource sectors, resulting in de-industrialization.

When a central bank purchases foreign currency to resist nominal appreciation without sterilizing the liquidity injection (via open market bond sales or the Standing Deposit Facility), the domestic monetary base expands. The resulting rise in domestic money supply fuels domestic inflation relative to trading partners, which causes the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) to appreciate (rise) even if the nominal exchange rate remains unchanged.

ref: IMF Finance & Development 'Dutch Disease: Too Much of a Good Thing'; RBI Bulletin on REER

stem: With reference to External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) and the foreign exchange exposure of Indian corporates, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A domestic highway developer that raises US Dollar-denominated External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) while earning its entire revenue in Indian Rupees from domestic toll collections enjoys a 'natural hedge' against Rupee depreciation.

2. Through the adverse 'balance sheet effect', a sharp depreciation of the Indian Rupee inflates the Rupee value of unhedged foreign currency debt liabilities, eroding the net worth and debt-servicing capacity of domestic borrowers.

3. Under the Reserve Bank of India's prudential norms on Unhedged Foreign Currency Exposure (UFCE), commercial banks are required to maintain incremental provisioning and capital buffers for corporate borrowers whose unhedged currency mismatch poses potential credit risk.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: A 'natural hedge' exists only when a firm's foreign currency debt obligations are matched by foreign currency revenue streams (such as exports). Firms borrowing in foreign currency while earning solely in domestic Rupees face unhedged balance-sheet vulnerability when the Rupee depreciates.

exp.why: A 'natural hedge' occurs when an entity with foreign currency liabilities also generates regular foreign currency revenues (such as an IT or pharmaceutical exporter earning in US Dollars), so that higher Rupee debt-service costs during depreciation are offset by higher Rupee export realizations. A domestic infrastructure firm earning exclusively in Rupees while servicing USD debt has a classic currency mismatch (unhedged exposure), not a natural hedge.

Under the macroeconomic 'balance sheet effect', when the domestic currency depreciates, the local-currency value of foreign-currency-denominated principal and interest obligations rises immediately, while the Rupee value of domestic assets and revenues remains unchanged. This compresses corporate net worth and tightens financial conditions.

To prevent foreign exchange volatility from translating into banking sector Non-Performing Assets (NPAs), the RBI's Master Direction on Unhedged Foreign Currency Exposure mandates that banks assess the likely loss from exchange rate movements relative to a borrower's EBID (Earnings Before Interest and Depreciation) and hold incremental provisioning and capital requirements accordingly.

ref: RBI Master Direction on Unhedged Foreign Currency Exposure (UFCE); Financial Stability Report

stem: In the context of India's Balance of Payments and exchange rate management, which one of the following best explains why India maintains a calibrated and partial approach to Capital Account Convertibility while upholding full Current Account Convertibility?

opts.A: India's acceptance of Article VIII obligations of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) legally mandates unrestricted convertibility for cross-border debt capital flows while permitting quantitative restrictions on current account invisibles.
opts.B: Full current account convertibility requires the Reserve Bank of India to maintain a rigid fixed exchange rate peg against the US Dollar, whereas partial capital account convertibility allows the Rupee to float without intervention.
opts.C: Unfettered freedom for short-term external debt inflows and unrestricted resident capital outflows can expose the domestic currency and financial system to sudden stops, speculative reversals, and boom-bust exchange rate volatility.
opts.D: Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, all current account transactions are statutorily prohibited unless specifically permitted, whereas all capital account transactions are freely permitted unless expressly restricted.

core: While India maintains full Current Account Convertibility under IMF Article VIII (since 1994) to facilitate trade and remittances, it practices calibrated Capital Account Convertibility with hierarchy-based controls on volatile debt flows and resident outflows to shield the Rupee from destabilizing speculative surges and sudden capital flight.

exp.why: Option C is correct because India follows a hierarchy of capital flows: preferring long-term, non-debt creating flows (like FDI) while maintaining macro-prudential ceilings on volatile debt flows (such as Foreign Portfolio Investment in debt and short-term External Commercial Borrowings) and annual caps on resident capital outflows under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS). This insulates the Rupee and domestic banking stability from 'sudden stops' and speculative capital flight. Option A is incorrect because IMF Article VIII governs Current Account Convertibility (adopted by India in August 1994), not capital account debt flows. Option B is incorrect because current account convertibility does not require a fixed exchange rate peg. Option D is incorrect because under Sections 5 and 6 of FEMA, 1999, the legal presumption is the exact opposite: current account transactions are freely permitted unless specifically restricted, whereas capital account transactions are prohibited unless expressly permitted by RBI/Government regulations.

ref: FEMA 1999 Sections 5 & 6; Tarapore Committee Reports on Capital Account Convertibility; RBI External Sector Publications

stem: With reference to the regulatory framework governing Exchange-Traded Currency Derivatives (ETCDs) involving the Indian Rupee on recognised domestic stock exchanges, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) regulations notified by the Reserve Bank of India, domestic retail participants are permitted to take purely speculative positions in Rupee currency derivatives without possessing any underlying contracted foreign exchange exposure.

2. Exchange-Traded Currency Derivatives involving the Indian Rupee on domestic stock exchanges (outside IFSC GIFT City) are compulsorily settled through the physical delivery of foreign currency notes at contract expiry rather than cash settlement in Indian Rupees.

3. The statutory authority to prescribe eligible participants and underlying exposure norms for Rupee foreign exchange derivatives vests exclusively with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), with no regulatory jurisdiction assigned to the Reserve Bank of India.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under FEMA, 1999 and the RBI Act, 1934, the RBI regulates the policy framework for all Rupee currency derivatives (both OTC and Exchange-Traded) and mandates that participants must possess a valid underlying contracted foreign exchange exposure so that the market serves genuine hedging needs rather than destabilizing currency speculation.

exp.why: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Foreign Exchange Derivative Contracts) Regulations and the RBI's Master Direction on Risk Management and Inter-Bank Dealings, any user participating in Exchange-Traded Currency Derivatives (ETCDs) involving the Indian Rupee must possess a valid underlying contracted foreign exchange exposure (such as genuine export/import receivables/payables or permitted capital account exposures) that has not already been hedged. While documentary submission is operationally simplified for positions up to USD 100 million across exchanges, the legal requirement of possessing a genuine underlying exposure to hedge is strictly mandatory to prevent speculative attacks on the Rupee.

Exchange-Traded Currency Derivatives (futures and options on USD-INR, EUR-INR, GBP-INR, and JPY-INR) traded on domestic stock exchanges are cash-settled in Indian Rupees based on the Financial Benchmarks India Pvt. Ltd. (FBIL) reference rate at contract expiry, and are not settled by physical delivery of foreign currency notes.

Under Section 45W of the RBI Act, 1934 and the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, the Reserve Bank of India holds statutory jurisdiction over foreign exchange derivative policy, permissible underlying exposures, and user eligibility for all Rupee currency derivatives, whereas SEBI regulates the exchange trading infrastructure, clearing corporations, margin collection, and broker surveillance.

ref: RBI Master Direction on Risk Management and Inter-Bank Dealings (2024); FEMA Foreign Exchange Derivative Contracts Regulations

stem: Consider the following institutional milestones in the historical evolution of India's exchange rate management regime:
items: 1. Introduction of the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) featuring a dual exchange rate
2. Transition to a unified, market-determined exchange rate system
3. Delinking of the Indian Rupee from the Pound Sterling and pegging it to a multi-currency basket of major trading partners
4. Acceptance of obligations under Article VIII of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Articles of Agreement for full Current Account Convertibility
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological sequence of the above milestones, from the earliest to the latest?
core: India transitioned gradually from a fixed par-value system to a multi-currency basket peg (1975), then to a transitional dual-rate regime under LERMS (1992), followed by a unified market-determined float (1993), before formally committing to IMF Article VIII Current Account Convertibility (1994). The dual-rate LERMS served as the essential bridge between administered exchange rates and a unified market rate.

exp.why: Following the balance of payments crisis and based on the High-Level Committee on Balance of Payments (chaired by Dr. C. Rangarajan), the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) was introduced in March 1992. Under this 40:60 dual exchange rate mechanism, 40% of foreign exchange earnings had to be surrendered at the official RBI rate (to finance essential imports like oil, fertilizers, and life-saving drugs) while 60% could be converted at market-determined rates.

In March 1993, the implicit tax on exporters under the dual-rate LERMS was abolished, and India transitioned to a unified, market-determined exchange rate system (managed float) where all foreign exchange receipts and payments were settled at market-determined rates.

After the collapse of the Bretton Woods par value system in 1971, the Rupee remained linked to the Pound Sterling until September 1975. To insulate the Rupee from the volatility of a single weakening currency, the RBI delinked the Rupee from the Pound Sterling in September 1975 and pegged it to an undisclosed basket of currencies of India's major trading partners.

Only after successfully stabilizing the unified market-determined exchange rate in March 1993 did India formally accept the obligations of Article VIII of the IMF Articles of Agreement in August 1994, committing not to impose restrictions on the making of payments and transfers for current international transactions without IMF approval.

ref: RBI Report on Currency and Finance; Economic Survey (External Sector Evolution)

stem: With reference to the computation and governance of the daily official USD/INR Reference Rate in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The daily USD/INR Reference Rate is administratively determined and notified by the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.
2. It is computed on the basis of the volume-weighted average of actual inter-bank spot market transactions executed on electronic trading platforms during a randomly selected time window.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: India's daily official Reference Rate for USD/INR (along with EUR, GBP, and JPY) is neither fixed by the Ministry of Finance nor polled via subjective quotes; it is computed and published by Financial Benchmarks India Pvt. Ltd. (FBIL), an independent benchmark administrator regulated by the RBI. FBIL calculates it using the volume-weighted average rate of actual inter-bank spot trades during a randomized 15-minute window.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The daily USD/INR Reference Rate is not determined by the Ministry of Finance. Since July 2018, Financial Benchmarks India Pvt. Ltd. (FBIL)—an independent benchmark administrator recognised and regulated by the Reserve Bank of India under Section 45W of the RBI Act, 1934—computes and publishes the daily Reference Rate.

Statement 2 is correct. To prevent market manipulation around a fixed fixing time, FBIL computes the USD/INR Reference Rate based on the volume-weighted average rate (VWAR) of actual inter-bank spot transactions executed on electronic trading platforms during a 15-minute window randomly chosen between 11:30 AM and 12:30 PM on every Mumbai business day.

ref: RBI Master Direction on Financial Benchmarks; FBIL Reference Rate Methodology Document

stem: Consider the following statements regarding fiscal policy and external sector dynamics:
items: Statement-I: A persistent structural increase in the government's fiscal deficit, where excessive domestic absorption relative to national savings spills over into higher net imports and a wider current account deficit, often exerts downward depreciation pressure on the domestic currency.

Statement-II: In India, the Union Government's fiscal deficit is financed predominantly through domestic rupee-denominated market borrowings rather than sovereign external debt issued in foreign currencies.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under the Twin Deficit Hypothesis derived from the national income identity (CA = [Sp - Ip] + [T - G]), fiscal dissaving that is not offset by higher net private savings causes total domestic absorption to exceed national income, widening the current account deficit and depreciating the currency. Separately, India's sovereign debt management strategy relies overwhelmingly on domestic rupee borrowings to insulate public finances from external currency risk.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. By the macroeconomic accounting identity (X - M) = (Sp - Ip) + (T - G), when a structural expansion in the fiscal deficit (G > T) occurs alongside an unchanged or negative private savings-investment gap (Ip > Sp), aggregate domestic absorption (C + I + G) exceeds national output.
